Address the elimination of factual shortcuts during the pre-training phase.
papers.abstract: Recent work has showcased the powerful capability of large language models (LLMs) in recalling knowledge and reasoning. However, the reliability of LLMs in combining these two capabilities into reasoning through multi-hop facts has not been widely explored. This paper systematically investigates the possibilities for LLMs to utilize shortcuts based on direct connections between the initial and terminal entities of multi-hop knowledge. We first explore the existence of factual shortcuts through Knowledge Neurons, revealing that: (i) the strength of factual shortcuts is highly correlated with the frequency of co-occurrence of initial and terminal entities in the pre-training corpora; (ii) few-shot prompting leverage more shortcuts in answering multi-hop questions compared to chain-of-thought prompting. Then, we analyze the risks posed by factual shortcuts from the perspective of multi-hop knowledge editing. Analysis shows that approximately 20% of the failures are attributed to shortcuts, and the initial and terminal entities in these failure instances usually have higher co-occurrences in the pre-training corpus. Finally, we propose erasing shortcut neurons to mitigate the associated risks and find that this approach significantly reduces failures in multiple-hop knowledge editing caused by shortcuts.

papers.title: RelEdit: Evaluating Conceptual Knowledge Editing in Language Models via Relational Reasoning
papers.research_question: How can we evaluate the impact of conceptual knowledge editing on a model's related beliefs and relational reasoning abilities?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces RelEdit, a benchmark for evaluating conceptual knowledge editing with a focus on relational reasoning, and finds that existing editing methods struggle with relational reasoning while a simple in-context baseline (MICE) performs well.
papers.conclusion: RelEdit fills a gap in evaluating conceptual knowledge editing by assessing relational reasoning, and in-context editing methods like MICE show promise for future research.
papers.key_findings:
Existing knowledge editing methods struggle to reason about related conceptual knowledge effectively.
Larger models are better equipped to handle the relational reasoning challenge.
Modifications between concepts that share similar semantic structures and superclasses facilitate the model's ability to update more related conceptual knowledge.
Instance-level evaluations reflect the ability of LLMs to maintain higher concept consistency by updating knowledge from related instances.
MICE, a memory-based in-context editing baseline, obtains the best scores on RelEdit, suggesting a promising research direction for model editing.
papers.limitation:
RelEdit does not explicitly verify the item-part relationships between concepts.
RelEdit does not include concepts with more than one meaning (polysemous concepts).
RelEdit relies on concepts extracted from DBpedia, which could be incomplete or outdated.
Evaluation of existing knowledge editing methods primarily focuses on limited models due to computational resources.
future_direction: Handling polysemous concepts in conceptual knowledge editing.
Utilizing the internal knowledge of language models instead of relying solely on external knowledge bases.
Evaluating on more models and larger scales.
papers.abstract: The conceptual knowledge in Large Language Models (LLMs) can become outdated over time, and concept editing is often an option. Current evaluations on conceptual knowledge editing primarily focus on whether the definitions of concepts are successfully edited, neglecting the impact on the model's related beliefs. To address this gap, we introduce a benchmark called RelEdit, which includes criteria and questions to assess both concept-level and instance-level relational reasoning abilities of edited models. Our findings reveal that existing knowledge editing methods struggle to reason about related conceptual knowledge effectively. Additionally, we introduce a simple memory-based in-context editing baseline, MICE, which prompts the language model to generate answers that align with the stored edited concepts in external memory. In addition, we find that MICE obtains the best scores on our benchmark, suggesting a promising research direction for model editing. The code is available at https://github.com/ivanniu/RelEdit.

papers.title: Cross-Lingual Knowledge Editing in Large Language Models
papers.research_question: When we utilize source-language samples to edit a multi-lingual LLM, can the model reflect consistent behaviors when faced with a different target language?
papers.core_contribution: This paper explores the cross-lingual effect of knowledge editing in LLMs, introduces the Bi-ZsRE dataset, and shows that existing knowledge editing methods struggle to transfer edited knowledge across languages.
papers.conclusion: Cross-lingual knowledge editing remains challenging, as current methods fail to transfer knowledge effectively across languages and show inconsistent behaviors.
papers.key_findings:
Language modeling gaps across different languages influence the efficiency of knowledge editing.
It is still hard for existing knowledge editing methods to transfer the edited knowledge from one language to another in a multi-lingual LLM.
When editing LLMs in a language, the model performance on the irrelevant examples in other languages could also be influenced, resulting in low cross-lingual locality.
Portability (reasoning based on edited knowledge) is extremely limited in both languages, indicating methods only memorize superficial wording changes.
Not all knowledge editing methods are equally sensitive to the choice of editing language; IKE performs well across languages due to in-context learning.
papers.limitation:
Bi-ZsRE only involves English and Chinese, limiting analysis across different language families.
The backbones used are several LLMs with 7B parameters; analysis on larger models is left for future work.
future_direction: Extend Bi-ZsRE to more languages for more comprehensive analyses.
Explore knowledge editing on LLMs with more parameters (e.g., 13B and 70B).
Explore more effective methods or design more reasonable training paradigms to let LLMs go beyond memorizing superficial wording changes.

papers.title: STEAM: A Semantic-Level Knowledge Editing Framework for Large Language Models
papers.research_question: How can knowledge editing methods be improved to ensure semantic coherence and integration of updated facts into the model's knowledge structure?
papers.core_contribution: STEAM is a semantic-level knowledge editing framework that enhances the integration of updated knowledge into the model's latent space, improving reasoning ability and semantic coherence.
papers.conclusion: STEAM demonstrates that semantic-level alignment improves reasoning capabilities and semantic coherence in knowledge editing, highlighting the importance of latent-space integration.
papers.key_findings:
Edited knowledge in conventional methods is encoded as isolated residual streams, separate from pre-existing knowledge.
Edited knowledge triggers shortcut-like activations that bypass the model's natural reasoning process.
STEAM improves portability and consistency in knowledge editing across multiple models.
STEAM enhances semantic alignment in the latent space, leading to better integration.
The framework is effective in both single and batch editing scenarios.
papers.limitation:
Dependence on external knowledge sources like Wikidata, which may be difficult for new or less-known entities.
Anchor construction may not fully reflect how language models internally structure knowledge.
future_direction: More systematic strategies for anchor construction and deeper investigation of knowledge inference mechanisms.
papers.abstract: Large Language Models store extensive factual knowledge acquired during large-scale pre-training. However, this knowledge is inherently static, reflecting only the state of the world at the time of training. Knowledge editing has emerged as a promising solution for updating outdated or incorrect facts without full retraining. However, most existing locate-and-edit methods primarily focus on token-level likelihood optimization without addressing semantic coherence. Our analysis reveals that such edited knowledge is often encoded as isolated residual streams in the model's latent space, distinct from pre-existing knowledge and bypassing natural reasoning process. To address this, we propose \textsc{Steam}, a semantic-level knowledge editing framework that enhances integration of updated knowledge into the model's knowledge structure. \textsc{Steam} first identifies target representations as semantic anchors for the updated factual association, then guides the internal representation of the edited fact towards these anchors through an alignment loss during optimization. Experimental results demonstrate that \textsc{Steam} improves model's ability to reason with edited knowledge and enhances semantic coherence, underscoring the importance of latent-space alignment for reliable and coherent knowledge editing. The code is available at https://github.com/GY-Jeong/STEAM.

papers.title: A Dual-Axis Taxonomy of Knowledge Editing for LLMs: From Mechanisms to Functions
papers.core_contribution: This survey introduces a novel function-based taxonomy for knowledge editing in LLMs, complementing existing mechanism-based taxonomies, to provide a more holistic view of the field.
papers.conclusion: Knowledge editing is an efficient alternative to retraining for updating LLMs, and this survey provides a comprehensive review by analyzing the field along mechanism and function axes, highlighting future challenges for adaptive, scalable, and secure editors.
papers.key_findings:
Knowledge editing methods can be categorized into parameter-modifying and parameter-preserving mechanisms.
The effectiveness of an editing method depends on the type of knowledge being edited (factual, temporal, conceptual, commonsense, social).
Current methods are primarily designed for factual knowledge and struggle with more complex knowledge types like commonsense and social knowledge.
There is a trade-off between locality and generalization in knowledge editing.
The field lacks theoretical foundations and faces challenges in scalability and robustness.
papers.limitation:
The survey represents a snapshot of research primarily published by mid-2025 and may not include very recent work.
The survey prioritizes categorization and synthesis over deep technical analysis of every individual method.
The survey does not provide a detailed comparison with related fields such as continual learning or parameter-efficient fine-tuning.
The survey does not introduce new empirical results or perform controlled, head-to-head comparisons of methods.
future_direction: Towards optimization-free and runtime editing.
Automating the discovery of knowledge to edit.
Enhancing robustness and security of edited models.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) acquire vast knowledge from large text corpora, but this information can become outdated or inaccurate. Since retraining is computationally expensive, knowledge editing offers an efficient alternative -- modifying internal knowledge without full retraining. These methods aim to update facts precisely while preserving the model's overall capabilities. While existing surveys focus on the mechanism of editing (e.g., parameter changes vs. external memory), they often overlook the function of the knowledge being edited. This survey introduces a novel, complementary function-based taxonomy to provide a more holistic view. We examine how different mechanisms apply to various knowledge types -- factual, temporal, conceptual, commonsense, and social -- highlighting how editing effectiveness depends on the nature of the target knowledge. By organizing our review along these two axes, we map the current landscape, outline the strengths and limitations of existing methods, define the problem formally, survey evaluation tasks and datasets, and conclude with open challenges and future directions.

papers.title: Locate-then-edit for Multi-hop Factual Recall under Knowledge Editing
papers.research_question: Why do existing locate-then-edit knowledge editing methods fail on multi-hop factual recall tasks, and how can they be improved by editing both shallow and deep MLP layers?
papers.core_contribution: The paper identifies that in multi-hop tasks, LLMs retrieve knowledge from deeper MLP layers, unlike single-hop tasks, and proposes IFMET, a locate-then-edit method that edits both shallow and deep layers using multi-hop prompts, significantly improving multi-hop factual recall.
papers.conclusion: IFMET effectively edits knowledge in both shallow and deep MLP layers, overcoming limitations of previous methods and leading to significant improvements in multi-hop factual recall tasks.
papers.key_findings:
In multi-hop scenarios, implicit subject information accumulates before the final answer at the last token position, unlike single-hop where subject is explicit.
The implicit subject has causal effects on the final answer in multi-hop reasoning, as shown by intervention experiments.
Knowledge is retrieved from deeper MLP layers in multi-hop tasks, while from shallow layers in single-hop.
Existing locate-then-edit methods fail on multi-hop tasks because they only edit shallow layers, leaving deeper layers unchanged.
IFMET successfully edits both shallow and deep MLP layers using single-hop and multi-hop prompts, improving multi-hop accuracy.
papers.abstract: The locate-then-edit paradigm has shown significant promise for knowledge editing (KE) in Large Language Models (LLMs). While previous methods perform well on single-hop fact recall tasks, they consistently struggle with multi-hop factual recall tasks involving newly edited knowledge. In this paper, leveraging tools in mechanistic interpretability, we first identify that in multi-hop tasks, LLMs tend to retrieve knowledge with implicit subject information from deeper MLP layers, unlike single-hop tasks, which rely on shallow layers. This distinction explains the poor performance of current methods in multi-hop queries, as they primarily focus on editing shallow layers with single-hop edit prompts, leaving deeper layers unchanged. To address this, we propose IFMET, a novel locate-then-edit KE approach designed to edit both shallow and deep MLP layers. Beyond single-hop editing prompts, IFMET further incorporates multi-hop editing prompts to locate and modify knowledge across different stages of reasoning. Experimental results demonstrate that IFMET significantly improves performance on multi-hop factual recall tasks, overcoming the limitations of previous locate-then-edit methods

papers.title: Precise Localization of Memories: A Fine-grained Neuron-level Knowledge Editing Technique for LLMs
papers.research_question: How can we improve the locality of knowledge editing in LLMs by moving from causal tracing to neuron-level localization?
papers.core_contribution: FiNE is a neuron-level knowledge editing method that improves editing locality by precisely identifying and modifying neurons in FFNs, overcoming the over-reliance on subject entities in previous causal tracing methods.
papers.conclusion: FiNE advances knowledge localization and editing in LLMs by providing a neuron-level approach that improves locality and efficiency, paving the way for more reliable knowledge management.
papers.key_findings:
Existing locate-then-edit methods based on causal tracing are overly subject-driven and neglect relations, leading to poor editing locality.
FiNE's neuron-level localization provides more precise knowledge localization than causal tracing.
FiNE achieves better locality scores and efficiency compared to existing methods like ROME, MEMIT, and PMET.
FiNE maintains high edit success and portability while significantly improving locality.
Ablation studies show that neuron localization and layer freezing are important components of FiNE.
papers.limitation: The safety of edits cannot be ensured, and there is potential for misuse such as introducing malicious misinformation or bias.
papers.abstract: Knowledge editing aims to update outdated information in Large Language Models (LLMs). A representative line of study is locate-then-edit methods, which typically employ causal tracing to identify the modules responsible for recalling factual knowledge about entities. However, we find these methods are often sensitive only to changes in the subject entity, leaving them less effective at adapting to changes in relations. This limitation results in poor editing locality, which can lead to the persistence of irrelevant or inaccurate facts, ultimately compromising the reliability of LLMs. We believe this issue arises from the insufficient precision of knowledge localization. To address this, we propose a Fine-grained Neuron-level Knowledge Editing (FiNE) method that enhances editing locality without affecting overall success rates. By precisely identifying and modifying specific neurons within feed-forward networks, FiNE significantly improves knowledge localization and editing. Quantitative experiments demonstrate that FiNE efficiently achieves better overall performance compared to existing techniques, providing new insights into the localization and modification of knowledge within LLMs.

papers.title: Knowledge Neurons in Pretrained Transformers
papers.research_question: How is factual knowledge stored in pretrained Transformers?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces the concept of knowledge neurons and a gradient-based attribution method to identify them in pretrained Transformers, demonstrating their role in storing factual knowledge and enabling model editing.
papers.conclusion: The paper demonstrates that factual knowledge in pretrained Transformers is stored in specific neurons (knowledge neurons) within feed-forward networks, and these neurons can be identified and manipulated to edit knowledge.
papers.key_findings:
Knowledge neurons identified by the proposed attribution method are positively correlated with the expression of specific factual knowledge.
Suppressing or amplifying the activation of identified knowledge neurons significantly decreases or increases the probability of the correct answer, respectively.
Knowledge neurons are more activated by prompts expressing their corresponding fact than by control prompts.
Knowledge neurons can be used to update or erase specific factual knowledge in the model with minimal impact on other knowledge.
papers.limitation:
Examines knowledge neurons based on the fill-in-the-blank cloze task, while knowledge can be expressed in more implicit ways.
Interactions between knowledge neurons remain underexplored.
Focuses on factual knowledge for ease of evaluation, though the method is applicable to other knowledge types.
Uses single-word blanks in cloze queries, requiring extension to multi-word answers.
future_direction: Investigate whether Transformers can utilize stored knowledge in a generalized way, such as for reasoning.
Explore interactions between knowledge neurons.
Extend the method to other types of knowledge beyond factual knowledge.
Extend to multi-word blanks in cloze queries.
Investigate knowledge neurons in multilingual pretrained Transformers.
papers.abstract: Large-scale pretrained language models are surprisingly good at recalling factual knowledge presented in the training corpus. In this paper, we present preliminary studies on how factual knowledge is stored in pretrained Transformers by introducing the concept of knowledge neurons. Specifically, we examine the fill-in-the-blank cloze task for BERT. Given a relational fact, we propose a knowledge attribution method to identify the neurons that express the fact. We find that the activation of such knowledge neurons is positively correlated to the expression of their corresponding facts. In our case studies, we attempt to leverage knowledge neurons to edit (such as update, and erase) specific factual knowledge without fine-tuning. Our results shed light on understanding the storage of knowledge within pretrained Transformers. The code is available at https://github.com/Hunter-DDM/knowledge-neurons.

papers.title: Tracing Multilingual Factual Knowledge Acquisition in Pretraining
papers.research_question: How do factual recall and crosslingual consistency evolve during pretraining in large language models?
papers.core_contribution: This work traces the development of multilingual factual recall and crosslingual consistency during pretraining, identifying two primary pathways: frequency-driven learning (dominant and language-agnostic) and crosslingual transfer (limited and constrained to certain relation types).
papers.conclusion: The study reveals that multilingual factual knowledge acquisition in LLMs is driven by two distinct pathways: frequency-driven learning and crosslingual transfer, with the former being dominant and the latter limited in scale and scope.
papers.key_findings:
Multilingual factual recall develops progressively during pretraining, with English and distant languages converging early, while similar-script languages improve with extended training.
Fact frequency in the pretraining corpus is a strong predictor of factual recall accuracy across languages, with high-frequency facts more likely to be recalled correctly.
Crosslingual transfer enables correct recall of some low-frequency facts in non-English languages, primarily via high-frequency English counterparts, but the effect is limited and emerges early in pretraining.
Script similarity (e.g., Latin script) plays a more important role than language family in sustained improvements and crosslingual consistency.
The relationship between fact frequency and recall accuracy emerges early in pretraining and strengthens over time.
papers.limitation:
The scale of crosslingual transfer is limited and typically constrained to relation types involving named entities.
Fact frequency approximation may be ambiguous for languages sharing scripts (e.g., English and French), leading to aggregated counts that might not reflect language-specific frequencies.
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) are capable of recalling multilingual factual knowledge present in their pretraining data. However, most studies evaluate only the final model, leaving the development of factual recall and crosslingual consistency throughout pretraining largely unexplored. In this work, we trace how factual recall and crosslingual consistency evolve during pretraining, focusing on OLMo-7B as a case study. We find that both accuracy and consistency improve over time for most languages. We show that this improvement is primarily driven by the fact frequency in the pretraining corpus: more frequent facts are more likely to be recalled correctly, regardless of language. Yet, some low-frequency facts in non-English languages can still be correctly recalled. Our analysis reveals that these instances largely benefit from crosslingual transfer of their English counterparts -- an effect that emerges predominantly in the early stages of pretraining. We pinpoint two distinct pathways through which multilingual factual knowledge acquisition occurs: (1) frequency-driven learning, which is dominant and language-agnostic, and (2) crosslingual transfer, which is limited in scale and typically constrained to relation types involving named entities. We release our code and data to facilitate further research at https://github.com/cisnlp/multilingual-fact-tracing.

papers.title: Language Representation Projection: Can We Transfer Factual Knowledge across Languages in Multilingual Language Models?
papers.research_question: Can cross-lingual alignment of representation spaces enable factual knowledge transfer across languages in multilingual pretrained language models?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes LRP2, a parameter-free method that projects language representations to align spaces, enabling effective cross-lingual factual knowledge transfer in multilingual models.
papers.conclusion: LRP2 enables factual knowledge transfer from English to non-English languages by aligning representation spaces, and analysis shows it enhances knowledge neuron overlap.
papers.key_findings:
LRP2 significantly improves factual knowledge retrieval accuracy and cross-lingual transferability across diverse non-English languages.
LRP2 affects the alignment of representation spaces, bringing non-English representations closer to English and then back.
LRP2 enhances the overlap of knowledge neurons between English and non-English languages.
Cross-lingual knowledge neurons exist in multilingual pretrained language models.
Different languages necessitate varying optimal layer settings for LRP2 to achieve best transferability.
papers.limitation:
The effectiveness of LRP2 heavily relies on the inherent capabilities of multilingual pretrained language models.
Experiments are limited to two relatively small models due to limited compute resources.
future_direction: Investigate LRP2 on larger language models with more compute resources.
papers.abstract: Multilingual pretrained language models serve as repositories of multilingual factual knowledge. Nevertheless, a substantial performance gap of factual knowledge probing exists between high-resource languages and low-resource languages, suggesting limited implicit factual knowledge transfer across languages in multilingual pretrained language models. This paper investigates the feasibility of explicitly transferring relatively rich factual knowledge from English to non-English languages. To accomplish this, we propose two parameter-free $\textbf{L}$anguage $\textbf{R}$epresentation $\textbf{P}$rojection modules (LRP2). The first module converts non-English representations into English-like equivalents, while the second module reverts English-like representations back into representations of the corresponding non-English language. Experimental results on the mLAMA dataset demonstrate that LRP2 significantly improves factual knowledge retrieval accuracy and facilitates knowledge transferability across diverse non-English languages. We further investigate the working mechanism of LRP2 from the perspectives of representation space and cross-lingual knowledge neuron.

papers.title: Assessing Knowledge Editing in Language Models via Relation Perspective
papers.research_question: Whether existing entity-centric knowledge editing methods are suitable for relation-centric editing, and where relation knowledge is stored in transformers.
papers.core_contribution: Introduces a new benchmark for relation-based knowledge editing (RaKE) and shows that existing editing methods underperform on relation editing because they only modify the FFN, while relation knowledge is also stored in attention layers.
papers.conclusion: Current editing methods are insufficient for relation-based editing because they focus only on the FFN and ignore the attention layer, which also stores relation knowledge.
papers.key_findings:
Existing knowledge editing methods perform significantly worse on relation-based editing compared to entity-based editing.
Relation knowledge is stored not only in the feed-forward network (FFN) but also in the attention layers of transformers.
papers.limitation:
The RaKE dataset lacks an assessment of relation specificity performance.
There is a lack of specific methods for editing relations.
future_direction: Explore the correlation and differences between entity and relation knowledge in language models.
Develop relation-based editing methods that also modify the attention module.
papers.abstract: Knowledge Editing (KE) for modifying factual knowledge in Large Language Models (LLMs) has been receiving increasing attention. However, existing knowledge editing methods are entity-centric, and it is unclear whether this approach is suitable for a relation-centric perspective. To address this gap, this paper constructs a new benchmark named RaKE, which focuses on Relation based Knowledge Editing. In this paper, we establish a suite of innovative metrics for evaluation and conduct comprehensive experiments involving various knowledge editing baselines. We notice that existing knowledge editing methods exhibit the potential difficulty in their ability to edit relations. Therefore, we further explore the role of relations in factual triplets within the transformer. Our research results confirm that knowledge related to relations is not only stored in the FFN network but also in the attention layers. This provides experimental support for future relation-based knowledge editing methods.

papers.title: Balancing Knowledge Updates: Toward Unified Modular Editing in LLMs
papers.research_question: How can knowledge editing in LLMs be improved by jointly updating both MLP and Attention modules, rather than focusing solely on MLP modules?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces IntAttn-Edit, a novel knowledge editing method that jointly updates both MLP and Attention modules using a knowledge balancing strategy, which proportionally allocates update magnitudes based on each module's measured contribution to knowledge storage.
papers.conclusion: IntAttn-Edit addresses the limitation of knowledge residuals in existing methods by jointly editing MLP and Attention modules, leading to more balanced and comprehensive knowledge updates that outperform existing approaches.
papers.key_findings:
Attention modules play a substantial role in factual knowledge storage and retrieval, especially in earlier layers, functioning as key-value associative memory structures.
IntAttn-Edit consistently outperforms existing editing baselines (e.g., ROME, MEMIT, AlphaEdit) on benchmarks like ZsRE and WikiData counterfact, achieving higher edit success and portability.
The proposed knowledge balancing strategy, which dynamically allocates update magnitudes between MLP and Attn modules based on their causal contributions, maintains editing performance within an optimal range.
Updating only a subset of knowledge-storage modules (e.g., only MLP) can leave residual outdated knowledge, which IntAttn-Edit mitigates by jointly editing both modules.
Extensive experiments show IntAttn-Edit delivers superior results across different batch sizes and models while maintaining high locality and fluency.
papers.abstract: Knowledge editing has emerged as an efficient approach for updating factual knowledge in large language models (LLMs). It typically locates knowledge storage modules and then modifies their parameters. However, most existing methods focus on the weights of multilayer perceptron (MLP) modules, which are often identified as the main repositories of factual information. Other components, such as attention (Attn) modules, are often ignored during editing. This imbalance can leave residual outdated knowledge and limit editing effectiveness. We perform comprehensive knowledge localization experiments on advanced LLMs and find that Attn modules play a substantial role in factual knowledge storage and retrieval, especially in earlier layers. Based on these insights, we propose IntAttn-Edit, a method that extends the associative memory paradigm to jointly update both MLP and Attn modules. Our approach uses a knowledge balancing strategy that allocates update magnitudes in proportion to each module's measured contribution to knowledge storage. Experiments on standard benchmarks show that IntAttn-Edit achieves higher edit success, better generalization, and stronger knowledge preservation than prior methods. Further analysis shows that the balancing strategy keeps editing performance within an optimal range across diverse settings.

papers.title: Paths Not Taken: Understanding and Mending the Multilingual Factual Recall Pipeline
papers.research_question: Why do multilingual large language models exhibit factual inconsistencies across languages, and how can these failures be understood and mended?
papers.core_contribution: The paper uncovers a multilingual factual recall pipeline where LLMs use an English-centric mechanism and then translate answers, and introduces two vector interventions to fix errors in translation and recall, significantly improving cross-lingual factual consistency.
papers.conclusion: Mechanistic insights into the multilingual processing pipeline can be used to design targeted, training-free interventions that direct the model toward better internal paths, unlocking latent multilingual capabilities and improving factual consistency.
papers.key_findings:
Multilingual LLMs employ a pipeline where factual information is first retrieved in English using intermediate English-centric mechanisms, followed by translation into the target language in later layers.
Two primary failure points cause cross-lingual inconsistencies: insufficient engagement of the reliable English-centric recall mechanism, and incorrect translation from English back to the target language.
A translation difference vector intervention, derived from the activation difference between explicit translation and fact-recall tasks, steers the model to use more effective translation components, improving conversion correctness.
A recall task vector intervention, extracted from in-context learning examples, promotes the engagement of English-centric factual recall components (like relation propagation and answer extraction) for multilingual prompts.
Combining both interventions leads to substantial improvements in factual recall accuracy, boosting performance by up to 37.6 percentage points for the lowest-performing language and an average gain of 19.04 points across all evaluated languages.
papers.limitation: The study is limited to five non-English languages and ten relations on a single model (Llama-3.2-3B).
future_direction: Expanding the investigation to more diverse language families and syntactic structures.
Quantifying how the findings apply to relations of varying complexity or different models.
Developing automated methods to identify such weaknesses and implement corresponding solutions.
papers.abstract: Multilingual large language models (LLMs) often exhibit factual inconsistencies across languages, with significantly better performance in factual recall tasks in English than in other languages. The causes of these failures, however, remain poorly understood. Using mechanistic analysis techniques, we uncover the underlying pipeline that LLMs employ, which involves using the English-centric factual recall mechanism to process multilingual queries and then translating English answers back into the target language. We identify two primary sources of error: insufficient engagement of the reliable English-centric mechanism for factual recall, and incorrect translation from English back into the target language for the final answer. To address these vulnerabilities, we introduce two vector interventions, both independent of languages and datasets, to redirect the model toward better internal paths for higher factual consistency. Our interventions combined increase the recall accuracy by over 35 percent for the lowest-performing language. Our findings demonstrate how mechanistic insights can be used to unlock latent multilingual capabilities in LLMs.

papers.title: Knowledge Editing for Large Language Model with Knowledge Neuronal Ensemble
papers.research_question: How can knowledge editing in large language models be improved to address challenges of parameter localization coupling, imprecise localization, and insufficient layer-wise dynamic interaction?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces the Knowledge Neuronal Ensemble (KNE) method for knowledge editing in LLMs, which localizes neurons via gradient attribution and edits them collectively, improving accuracy and efficiency while maintaining model performance.
papers.conclusion: The KNE method addresses limitations of current knowledge editing techniques and demonstrates superior performance across multiple datasets, with reduced computational overhead.
papers.key_findings:
KNE outperforms baseline methods (FT, FT-L, AdaLoRA, ROME, MEMIT) in edit success, portability, and locality on multiple datasets.
Editing the FFN module (especially the value layer) yields better edit success and portability, while mapping layers (mlp.gate_proj, mlp.up_proj, self_attn.q_proj) are important for locality and fluency.
Similar knowledge is stored in similar locations, allowing partial localization (e.g., 200 knowledge points) to achieve good performance, reducing computational cost.
There is a trade-off between the number of parameters edited and performance: more parameters improve edit success and portability but harm locality.
KNE supports batch editing with acceptable trade-offs in performance.
papers.limitation:
The performance of the KNE method heavily depends on the quality of the selected knowledge set.
The finding that modifying the key layer in the FFN module yields favorable results in terms of locality requires deeper theoretical analysis and explanation.
future_direction: Incorporate more refined knowledge selection mechanisms to enhance the precision of knowledge editing while minimizing disruption to the model's existing capabilities.
Further investigate the knowledge transmission mechanisms between different layers of models to systematically understand and optimize knowledge storage and editing processes.
papers.abstract: As real-world knowledge is constantly evolving, ensuring the timeliness and accuracy of a model's knowledge is crucial. This has made knowledge editing in large language models increasingly important. However, existing knowledge editing methods face several challenges, including parameter localization coupling, imprecise localization, and a lack of dynamic interaction across layers. In this paper, we propose a novel knowledge editing method called Knowledge Neuronal Ensemble (KNE). A knowledge neuronal ensemble represents a group of neurons encoding specific knowledge, thus mitigating the issue of frequent parameter modification caused by coupling in parameter localization. The KNE method enhances the precision and accuracy of parameter localization by computing gradient attribution scores for each parameter at each layer. During the editing process, only the gradients and losses associated with the knowledge neuronal ensemble are computed, with error backpropagation performed accordingly, ensuring dynamic interaction and collaborative updates among parameters. Experimental results on three widely used knowledge editing datasets show that the KNE method significantly improves the accuracy of knowledge editing and achieves, or even exceeds, the performance of the best baseline methods in portability and locality metrics.

papers.title: Untying the Reversal Curse via Bidirectional Language Model Editing
papers.research_question: Can edited large language models recall editing knowledge bidirectionally, i.e., in both the direction of editing and the reverse direction?
papers.core_contribution: This paper introduces bidirectional language model editing, proposing a benchmark (BAKE) and a method (BIRD) to mitigate the reversal curse, enabling edited models to recall facts in both forward and reverse directions.
papers.conclusion: Bidirectional language model editing is crucial, and the proposed BIRD method effectively mitigates the reversal curse, improving the reversibility of edited models.
papers.key_findings:
Existing model editing methods and LLMs suffer from the reversal curse, performing well in the editing direction but catastrophically failing in the reverse direction.
The proposed BIRD method improves the ability of edited models to recall facts in the reverse direction while maintaining performance in the editing direction.
The reversal curse in model editing is a significant and previously unexplored problem, indicating that current editing methods do not fully understand injected knowledge.
papers.limitation:
BIRD does not perform well in Reverse-QA Score (RQS).
The work focuses on factual knowledge and does not investigate other types of learned beliefs (logical, spatial, numerical).
The research focuses on autoregressive models, and non-autoregressive models are not explored.
The work uses editing methods that modify model parameters, while methods that preserve parameters are not considered.
future_direction: Developing more efficient bidirectional editing methods.
Extending the research to other types of knowledge (logical, spatial, numerical).
Exploring bidirectional editing for non-autoregressive models and methods that preserve model parameters.
papers.abstract: Recent studies have demonstrated that large language models (LLMs) store massive factual knowledge within their parameters. But existing LLMs are prone to hallucinate unintended text due to false or outdated knowledge. Since retraining LLMs is resource intensive, there has been a growing interest in the concept of model editing. Despite the emergence of benchmarks and approaches, these unidirectional editing and evaluation have failed to explore the reversal curse. Intuitively, if "The capital of France is" is edited to be a counterfact "London" within a model, then it should be able to naturally reason and recall the reverse fact, i.e., "London is the capital of" followed by "France" instead of "England". In this paper, we study bidirectional language model editing, aiming to provide rigorous model editing evaluation to assess if edited LLMs can recall the editing knowledge bidirectionally. A new evaluation metric of reversibility is introduced, and a benchmark dubbed as Bidirectional Assessment for Knowledge Editing (BAKE) is constructed to evaluate the reversibility of edited models in recalling knowledge in the reverse direction of editing. We surprisingly observe that while current editing methods and LLMs can effectively recall editing facts in the direction of editing, they suffer serious deficiencies when evaluated in the reverse direction. To mitigate the reversal curse, a method named Bidirectionally Inversible Relationship moDeling (BIRD) is proposed. A set of editing objectives that incorporate bidirectional relationships between subject and object into the updated model weights are designed. Experiments show that BIRD improves the performance of four representative LLMs of different sizes via question answering and judgement.

papers.title: Evaluating Dependencies in Fact Editing for Language Models: Specificity and Implication Awareness
papers.research_question: This paper investigates how well existing knowledge editing methods for language models respect dependency constraints, specifically whether they can edit facts without affecting irrelevant ones (specificity) and whether they can correctly infer logical implications of edited facts (implication awareness).
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces a new evaluation protocol (establish-and-update) and dataset (DepEdit) for assessing knowledge editing methods in language models with respect to dependency constraints (specificity and implication awareness), and finds that existing methods are sensitive to surface form and perform poorly on implication awareness.
papers.conclusion: The paper concludes that current knowledge editing methods are limited in handling dependency constraints, especially implication awareness, and suggests that future work should develop methods that better incorporate logical dependencies.
papers.key_findings:
Existing knowledge editing methods (MEND, MEMIT) are sensitive to lexical variations and perform worse when questions are rephrased.
These methods struggle to update logical implications of edited facts, treating implications as unrelated knowledge.
Fine-tuning achieves high success rates but disrupts unrelated facts, while MEND and MEMIT better preserve unrelated facts.
Gradient similarity between updating premise facts and implications is low, similar to that between facts with similar surface forms.
External inference mechanisms (forward/backward chaining) can improve implication editing but may introduce inconsistencies.
papers.limitation:
DepEdit does not support evaluation of knowledge editing with complex logical operations such as quantification and probabilistic entailment.
Each knowledge set contains only one rule and avoids conflicts among facts and implications, which may not reflect real-world scenarios.
future_direction: Develop implication-aware knowledge editing methods inspired by knowledge base editing techniques.
Extend DepEdit to include multiple rules per knowledge set and handle conflicts.
Extend DepEdit to support complex logical operations like quantification and probabilistic entailment.
papers.abstract: The potential of using a large language model (LLM) as a knowledge base (KB) has sparked significant interest. To manage the knowledge acquired by LLMs, we need to ensure that the editing of learned facts respects internal logical constraints, which are known as dependency of knowledge. Existing work on editing LLMs has partially addressed the issue of dependency, when the editing of a fact should apply to its lexical variations without disrupting irrelevant ones. However, they neglect the dependency between a fact and its logical implications. We propose an evaluation protocol with an accompanying question-answering dataset, DepEdit, that provides a comprehensive assessment of the editing process considering the above notions of dependency. Our protocol involves setting up a controlled environment in which we edit facts and monitor their impact on LLMs, along with their implications based on If-Then rules. Extensive experiments on DepEdit show that existing knowledge editing methods are sensitive to the surface form of knowledge, and that they have limited performance in inferring the implications of edited facts.

papers.title: Benchmarking and Rethinking Knowledge Editing for Large Language Models
papers.research_question: How do knowledge editing methods perform in practice-oriented settings, including autoregressive inference and sequential editing? Can they help reasoning LLMs integrate new facts without degrading reasoning ability, and generalize from factual to event knowledge?
papers.core_contribution: This paper provides a comprehensive benchmarking study of knowledge editing methods, revealing that parameter-based editing methods perform poorly under realistic conditions (autoregressive inference, sequential editing), while a simple context-based baseline (SCR) consistently outperforms them.
papers.conclusion: Parameter-based knowledge editing methods have critical limitations in practical scenarios, while context-based reasoning approaches like SCR offer a more robust and promising alternative for updating knowledge in LLMs.
papers.key_findings:
Parameter-modification-based knowledge editing methods exhibit poor transferability and lose multi-hop reasoning capabilities under realistic evaluation settings.
As the number of edits increases, the performance of parameter-modification methods degrades sharply, making them impractical for real-world use.
After editing, LLMs often suffer significant declines in general performance, including loss of basic reasoning and processing abilities.
In-context learning and external memory methods (like SCR) demonstrate greater stability and robustness across editing scenarios.
Most parameter-modification methods struggle to handle complex event-level knowledge, while context-based methods generalize better.
papers.abstract: Knowledge editing aims to update the embedded knowledge within Large Language Models (LLMs). However, existing approaches, whether through parameter modification or external memory integration, often suffer from inconsistent evaluation objectives and experimental setups. To address this gap, we conduct a comprehensive benchmarking study. In addition to fact-level datasets, we introduce more complex event-based datasets and general-purpose datasets drawn from other tasks. Our evaluation covers both instruction-tuned and reasoning-oriented LLMs, under a realistic autoregressive inference setting rather than teacher-forced decoding. Beyond single-edit assessments, we also evaluate multi-edit scenarios to better reflect practical demands. We employ four evaluation dimensions, including portability, and compare all recent methods against a simple and straightforward baseline named Selective Contextual Reasoning (SCR). Empirical results reveal that parameter-based editing methods perform poorly under realistic conditions. In contrast, SCR consistently outperforms them across all settings. This study offers new insights into the limitations of current knowledge editing methods and highlights the potential of context-based reasoning as a more robust alternative.

papers.title: The Unreasonable Effectiveness of Model Merging for Cross-Lingual Transfer in LLMs
papers.research_question: How can modular approaches, such as model merging, improve cross-lingual transfer of mathematical reasoning capabilities to lower-resource languages in LLMs?
papers.core_contribution: Modular approaches, particularly model merging via Layer-Swapping, effectively improve cross-lingual transfer for mathematical reasoning in low-resource languages, and full fine-tuning followed by parameter resetting outperforms freezing parameters during training.
papers.conclusion: Imposing modularity through model merging is effective for cross-lingual transfer in low-data scenarios, with Layer-Swapping being particularly successful due to the linearity of task vectors and the benefits of full fine-tuning before selective resetting.
papers.key_findings:
All modular solutions (including Layer-Swapping and simultaneous partition SFT) outperform non-modular baselines in cross-lingual transfer for math.
Layer-Swapping, which merges separately trained experts, outperforms more coordinated multi-task fine-tuning approaches.
Full fine-tuning of all parameters followed by resetting unused parameters (via merging) is more effective than freezing those parameters from the start.
The success of Layer-Swapping is partly due to the linearity of task vectors in transformer layers, allowing seamless composition.
Parameter allocations based on prior interpretability work (e.g., top/bottom layers for language, middle layers for math) are effective for modular training.
papers.limitation: The improvements are small because the experiments start from instruction-tuned models that have already undergone extensive post-training, and the fine-tuning datasets are small.
future_direction: Explore more modular configurations and parameter allocation strategies.
Examine other tasks beyond mathematical reasoning.
Improve interpretability to better localize capabilities in LLMs.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) still struggle across tasks outside of high-resource languages. In this work, we investigate cross-lingual transfer to lower-resource languages where task-specific post-training data is scarce. Building on prior work, we first validate that the subsets of model parameters that matter most for mathematical reasoning and multilingual capabilities are distinctly non-overlapping. To exploit this implicit separability between task and target language parameterization, we develop and analyze numerous modular frameworks to improve the composition of the two during fine-tuning. These methods generally employ freezing parameters or post hoc model merging to assign math and language improvement to different key parts of the LLM. In the absence of in-language math data, we demonstrate that the modular approaches successfully improve upon baselines across three languages, four models, and two fine-tuning paradigms (full and LoRA). Furthermore, we identify the most consistently successful modular method to be fine-tuning separate language and math experts and model merging via Layer-Swapping, somewhat surprisingly. We offer possible explanations for this result via recent works on the linearity of task vectors. We further explain this by empirically showing that reverting less useful fine-tuning updates after training often outperforms freezing them from the start.

papers.title: Everything is Editable: Extend Knowledge Editing to Unstructured Data in Large Language Models
papers.research_question: How to extend knowledge editing to unstructured data in large language models?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes UnKE, a method for editing unstructured knowledge in LLMs using non-local block key-value storage and cause-driven optimization.
papers.conclusion: UnKE effectively edits unstructured knowledge in LLMs and surpasses strong baselines.
papers.key_findings:
UnKE outperforms existing baselines on unstructured knowledge editing benchmark UnKEBench.
UnKE demonstrates robust batch editing and sequential editing capabilities.
Knowledge in LLMs is stored non-locally, contradicting the local storage hypothesis.
Term-driven optimization is not robust for unstructured knowledge editing.
UnKE also performs well on structured knowledge editing benchmarks.
papers.limitation: Potential misuse by malicious actors to inject harmful information into LLMs
papers.abstract: Recent knowledge editing methods have primarily focused on modifying structured knowledge in large language models. However, this task setting overlooks the fact that a significant portion of real-world knowledge is stored in an unstructured format, characterized by long-form content, noise, and a complex yet comprehensive nature. Techniques like "local layer key-value storage" and "term-driven optimization", as used in previous methods like MEMIT, are not effective for handling unstructured knowledge. To address these challenges, we propose a novel Unstructured Knowledge Editing method, namely UnKE, which extends previous assumptions in the layer dimension and token dimension. Firstly, in the layer dimension, we propose non-local block key-value storage to replace local layer key-value storage, increasing the representation ability of key-value pairs and incorporating attention layer knowledge. Secondly, in the token dimension, we replace "term-driven optimization" with "cause-driven optimization", which edits the last token directly while preserving context, avoiding the need to locate terms and preventing the loss of context information. Results on newly proposed unstructured knowledge editing dataset (UnKEBench) and traditional structured datasets demonstrate that UnKE achieves remarkable performance, surpassing strong baselines. In addition, UnKE has robust batch editing and sequential editing capabilities.

papers.title: Beyond the Rosetta Stone: Unification Forces in Generalization Dynamics
papers.research_question: What causes cross-lingual factual errors in language models, and how can we understand and improve cross-lingual transfer?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces a controlled 'Petri dish' methodology to study cross-lingual knowledge transfer dynamics, identifies a crucial early phase where models develop unified or separate representations across languages, and shows that unification predicts cross-lingual generalization.
papers.conclusion: Controlled settings can shed light on pre-training dynamics and suggest new directions for improving cross-lingual transfer in LLMs.
papers.key_findings:
Models undergo an early learning phase where they develop either unified or separate representations for the same facts across languages.
Unification of representations is essential for cross-lingual factual transfer.
The degree of unification depends on the mutual information between facts and training data language, and on how easy it is to extract the language feature.
Cross-lingual transfer can be improved without increasing parallel data by manipulating data distribution and tokenization to reduce the language feature's representational footprint.
A unification score, measuring similarity of representations across languages, strongly predicts cross-lingual factual recall accuracy.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) struggle with cross-lingual knowledge transfer: they hallucinate when asked in one language about facts expressed in a different language during training. This work introduces a controlled setting to study the causes and dynamics of this phenomenon by training small Transformer models from scratch on synthetic multilingual datasets. We identify a learning phase wherein a model develops either separate or unified representations of the same facts across languages, and show that unification is essential for cross-lingual transfer. We also show that the degree of unification depends on mutual information between facts and training data language, and on how easy it is to extract that language. Based on these insights, we develop methods to modulate the level of cross-lingual transfer by manipulating data distribution and tokenization, and we introduce metrics and visualizations to formally characterize their effects on unification. Our work shows how controlled settings can shed light on pre-training dynamics and suggests new directions for improving cross-lingual transfer in LLMs.

papers.title: Latent Knowledge Scalpel: Precise and Massive Knowledge Editing for Large Language Models
papers.research_question: How to enable precise and large-scale knowledge editing for large language models without compromising their general capabilities?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Latent Knowledge Scalpel (LKS), an LLM editor that uses a lightweight hyper-network to manipulate entity latent knowledge for precise and large-scale editing while preserving general abilities.
papers.conclusion: LKS enables precise and scalable knowledge editing in LLMs, highlighting the structured nature of entity representations and opening new possibilities for efficient updates.
papers.key_findings:
LKS outperforms other model editing methods in reliability, generality, and locality.
LKS can perform up to 10,000 simultaneous edits effectively.
LKS preserves the general abilities of LLMs, such as mathematical reasoning and sentiment analysis, even after large-scale editing.
Entity knowledge blocks in LLMs contain semantic information and internal representations retain syntactic structure.
Modifying intermediate layers yields higher effectiveness for knowledge editing.
papers.limitation: The Edit Scope Indicator incurs overhead by identifying entities, which can be mitigated by optimizing the entity recognition mechanism.
future_direction: Optimizing the entity recognition mechanism, e.g., by incorporating vector-level semantic matching or building an entity alias dictionary.
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) often retain inaccurate or outdated information from pre-training, leading to incorrect predictions or biased outputs during inference. While existing model editing methods can address this challenge, they struggle with editing large amounts of factual information simultaneously and may compromise the general capabilities of the models. In this paper, our empirical study demonstrates that it is feasible to edit the internal representations of LLMs and replace the entities in a manner similar to editing natural language inputs. Based on this insight, we introduce the Latent Knowledge Scalpel (LKS), an LLM editor that manipulates the latent knowledge of specific entities via a lightweight hypernetwork to enable precise and large-scale editing. Experiments conducted on Llama-2 and Mistral show even with the number of simultaneous edits reaching 10,000, LKS effectively performs knowledge editing while preserving the general abilities of the edited LLMs. Code is available at: https://github.com/Linuxin-xxx/LKS.

papers.title: Journey to the Center of the Knowledge Neurons: Discoveries of Language-Independent Knowledge Neurons and Degenerate Knowledge Neurons
papers.research_question: How is factual knowledge stored in multilingual pre-trained language models? Specifically, are there language-independent knowledge neurons and degenerate knowledge neurons?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces the Architecture-adapted Multilingual Integrated Gradients (AMIG) method for precise knowledge neuron localization and discovers two novel types of neurons: language-independent knowledge neurons, which store knowledge across languages, and degenerate knowledge neurons, which provide functional overlap for robust fact storage and can be used for fact-checking.
papers.conclusion: The paper concludes that their AMIG method enables precise knowledge localization and reveals two types of neurons that provide insights into knowledge storage, with language-independent neurons enabling cross-lingual editing and degenerate neurons enabling fact-checking.
papers.key_findings:
AMIG localizes knowledge neurons more precisely than previous methods, especially for Chinese datasets.
Knowledge neurons in m-BERT are primarily in the final layers, while in m-GPT they are distributed across early, middle, and final layers.
Language-independent knowledge neurons are concentrated in the final one or two layers and facilitate cross-lingual knowledge editing.
Degenerate knowledge neurons exist and can help PLMs detect wrong facts, improving fact-checking performance.
The existence of degenerate knowledge neurons is not dependent on multilingualism, as they are also found in monolingual models like BERT and GPT-2.
papers.abstract: Pre-trained language models (PLMs) contain vast amounts of factual knowledge, but how the knowledge is stored in the parameters remains unclear. This paper delves into the complex task of understanding how factual knowledge is stored in multilingual PLMs, and introduces the Architecture-adapted Multilingual Integrated Gradients method, which successfully localizes knowledge neurons more precisely compared to current methods, and is more universal across various architectures and languages. Moreover, we conduct an in-depth exploration of knowledge neurons, leading to the following two important discoveries: (1) The discovery of Language-Independent Knowledge Neurons, which store factual knowledge in a form that transcends language. We design cross-lingual knowledge editing experiments, demonstrating that the PLMs can accomplish this task based on language-independent neurons; (2) The discovery of Degenerate Knowledge Neurons, a novel type of neuron showing that different knowledge neurons can store the same fact. Its property of functional overlap endows the PLMs with a robust mastery of factual knowledge. We design fact-checking experiments, proving that the degenerate knowledge neurons can help the PLMs to detect wrong facts. Experiments corroborate these findings, shedding light on the mechanisms of factual knowledge storage in multilingual PLMs, and contribute valuable insights to the field. The code is available at https://github.com/heng840/AMIG.

papers.title: Are Knowledge and Reference in Multilingual Language Models Cross-Lingually Consistent?
papers.research_question: Do multilingual language models recall factual knowledge for coreferential statements in a similar manner across languages, how does the mechanism work, and which factors prevent model consistency in multilingual settings?
papers.core_contribution: The paper analyzes cross-lingual consistency of factual knowledge in multilingual models, identifying bottlenecks related to language characteristics and showing that explicit cross-lingual supervision (code-switching, word alignment) improves consistency more than scaling or instruction tuning.
papers.conclusion: The study highlights limitations in cross-lingual consistency of multilingual models and emphasizes the value of explicit cross-lingual alignment supervision and code-switching strategies for enhancing consistency.
papers.key_findings:
Cross-lingual consistency is lower for languages dissimilar to English in script, family, or geography.
A consistency bottleneck exists in specific middle layers of the models.
Vocabulary expansion offers only slight consistency improvements and relies on deep semantic alignment rather than shared scripts.
Code-switching training and cross-lingual word alignment objectives significantly improve consistency, while instruction tuning offers limited gains.
Activation patching on feed-forward neurons based on IG2 scores can partially calibrate consistency at test time, showing a causal relationship.
papers.abstract: Cross-lingual consistency should be considered to assess cross-lingual transferability, maintain the factuality of the model knowledge across languages, and preserve the parity of language model performance. We are thus interested in analyzing, evaluating, and interpreting cross-lingual consistency for factual knowledge. To facilitate our study, we examine multiple pretrained models and tuned models with code-mixed coreferential statements that convey identical knowledge across languages. Interpretability approaches are leveraged to analyze the behavior of a model in cross-lingual contexts, showing different levels of consistency in multilingual models, subject to language families, linguistic factors, scripts, and a bottleneck in cross-lingual consistency on a particular layer. Code-switching training and cross-lingual word alignment objectives show the most promising results, emphasizing the worthiness of cross-lingual alignment supervision and code-switching strategies for both multilingual performance and cross-lingual consistency enhancement. In addition, experimental results suggest promising result for calibrating consistency in the test time via activation patching.

papers.title: WilKE: Wise-Layer Knowledge Editor for Lifelong Knowledge Editing
papers.research_question: What causes performance degradation in lifelong knowledge editing, and how can it be addressed by selecting appropriate editing layers?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces WilKE, a knowledge editing method that selects editing layers based on pattern matching to mitigate toxicity buildup and flash in lifelong editing, significantly improving performance over state-of-the-art methods.
papers.conclusion: WilKE addresses the pattern unmatch problem in lifelong knowledge editing, significantly improving performance and providing valuable insights for future work.
papers.key_findings:
Current knowledge editing methods like ROME and MEMIT suffer from toxicity buildup and toxicity flash in lifelong editing, leading to performance degradation.
The primary cause of these issues is pattern unmatch, where predefined editing layers do not align with where knowledge is stored in the model.
WilKE selects editing layers based on the degree of pattern matching for different knowledge, reducing toxicity buildup and flash.
WilKE outperforms state-of-the-art methods in lifelong editing on GPT2-XL and GPT-J, with average improvements of 46.2% and 67.8% respectively.
The method demonstrates superior comprehensive performance in lifelong editing scenarios compared to existing approaches.
papers.limitation:
Knowledge may be distributed across multiple layers, leaving the question of how language models store knowledge still under explored.
Focus on factual knowledge assessment, which serves as a crucial entry point but may not cover other types of knowledge.
Due to computational constraints, no experiments were conducted on larger-scale language models.
Detecting match degree of specific knowledge across different layers incurs a certain time cost.
papers.abstract: Knowledge editing aims to rectify inaccuracies in large language models (LLMs) without costly retraining for outdated or erroneous knowledge. However, current knowledge editing methods primarily focus on single editing, failing to meet the requirements for lifelong editing. This study reveals a performance degradation encountered by knowledge editing in lifelong editing, characterized by toxicity buildup and toxicity flash, with the primary cause identified as pattern unmatch. We introduce a knowledge editing approach named Wise-Layer Knowledge Editor (WilKE), which selects editing layer based on the pattern matching degree of editing knowledge across different layers in language models. Experimental results demonstrate that, in lifelong editing, WilKE exhibits an average improvement of 46.2% and 67.8% on editing GPT2-XL and GPT-J relative to state-of-the-art knowledge editing methods.

papers.title: Understanding Language Model Circuits through Knowledge Editing
papers.research_question: How is knowledge structured within the critical subnetworks (circuits) of language models?
papers.core_contribution: The paper combines knowledge editing and circuit analysis to reveal that knowledge-intensive circuits exhibit 'confirmation bias' (resistance to editing), knowledge is distributed in circuits of intermediate size, circuits from different tasks overlap, and LayerNorm plays a larger role in circuits than previously assumed.
papers.conclusion: Combining knowledge editing and circuit analysis reveals novel properties of circuits, such as resistance to editing, distribution patterns, and the role of LayerNorm, supporting future explorations into model behaviors, bias removal, and interpretability.
papers.key_findings:
Knowledge-intensive circuits show stronger resistance to editing compared to their complementary parts, analogous to 'confirmation bias'.
Knowledge is neither extremely concentrated nor widely dispersed; ideal knowledge-bearing circuits likely contain between 5% and 50% of parameters.
Circuits extracted from different tasks (e.g., linguistic and knowledge-based) show non-negligible overlap.
LayerNorm components constitute a larger share of the extracted circuits than attention and MLP layers.
Complementary circuits are more susceptible to editing, suggesting potential for bias removal without compromising primary circuit performance.
papers.limitation:
Only the GPT-2 model was used.
Only fine-tuning model edit was investigated; alternative model editing methods can be explored.
Only a handful of text classification problems were investigated.
future_direction: Further investigation into the role and characteristics of complementary circuits.
Investigating the possibility of ideal circuits that can perform well for every specific task.
Exploring other techniques like ROME to edit complementary circuits without impacting primary circuits.
Creating more comprehensive datasets that capture a wider range of behaviors.
papers.abstract: Recent advances in language model interpretability have identified circuits, critical subnetworks that replicate model behaviors, yet how knowledge is structured within these crucial subnetworks remains opaque. To gain an understanding toward the knowledge in the circuits, we conduct systematic knowledge editing experiments on the circuits of the GPT-2 language model. Our analysis reveals intriguing patterns in how circuits respond to editing attempts, the extent of knowledge distribution across network components, and the architectural composition of knowledge-bearing circuits. These findings offer insights into the complex relationship between model circuits and knowledge representation, deepening the understanding of how information is organized within language models. Our findings offer novel insights into the ``meanings'' of the circuits, and introduce directions for further interpretability and safety research of language models.

papers.title: Knowledge Circuits in Pretrained Transformers
papers.research_question: How do transformers store and express knowledge through collaborative circuits of components such as attention heads and MLPs, and how can these circuits be used to analyze model behaviors and knowledge editing?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces knowledge circuits as a method to uncover how transformers store and express knowledge through collaborative components, and demonstrates their utility in analyzing knowledge editing and model behaviors like hallucinations and in-context learning.
papers.conclusion: Knowledge circuits provide a valuable framework for understanding how transformers store and express knowledge, and can inform the design of better knowledge editing methods.
papers.key_findings:
Knowledge circuits effectively capture knowledge representations, maintaining over 70% of original performance with less than 10% of the graph.
Knowledge is aggregated in early-to-middle layers and enhanced in later layers.
Special components like mover heads and relation heads are critical for information transfer and relational capture.
ROME editing incorporates information at the edited layer, while fine-tuning directly writes knowledge and dominates predictions.
Hallucinations occur when the circuit lacks effective mover heads or they select incorrect information.
papers.limitation:
Coarse granularity of circuits, not capturing fine-grained neuron-level behavior.
Logit lens method may have discrepancies between middle layers and output unembedding matrix.
future_direction: Finer-grained circuit analysis at the neuron level.
Developing more robust techniques to map intermediate representations to outputs (e.g., Attention Lens).
Investigating activation mechanisms of reused heads and polysemanticity.
papers.abstract: The remarkable capabilities of modern large language models are rooted in their vast repositories of knowledge encoded within their parameters, enabling them to perceive the world and engage in reasoning. The inner workings of how these models store knowledge have long been a subject of intense interest and investigation among researchers. To date, most studies have concentrated on isolated components within these models, such as the Multilayer Perceptrons and attention head. In this paper, we delve into the computation graph of the language model to uncover the knowledge circuits that are instrumental in articulating specific knowledge. The experiments, conducted with GPT2 and TinyLLAMA, have allowed us to observe how certain information heads, relation heads, and Multilayer Perceptrons collaboratively encode knowledge within the model. Moreover, we evaluate the impact of current knowledge editing techniques on these knowledge circuits, providing deeper insights into the functioning and constraints of these editing methodologies. Finally, we utilize knowledge circuits to analyze and interpret language model behaviors such as hallucinations and in-context learning. We believe the knowledge circuits hold potential for advancing our understanding of Transformers and guiding the improved design of knowledge editing. Code and data are available in https://github.com/zjunlp/KnowledgeCircuits.

papers.title: Editing Factual Knowledge in Language Models
papers.research_question: How can we edit factual knowledge in language models efficiently and reliably without retraining or fine-tuning?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces KNOWLEDGE EDITOR, a hyper-network-based method to edit factual knowledge in language models efficiently and reliably without retraining or fine-tuning, while preserving other knowledge and ensuring consistency across paraphrases.
papers.conclusion: KNOWLEDGE EDITOR provides an effective and reliable method for editing factual knowledge in language models, meeting desiderata of generality, reliability, and consistency.
papers.key_findings:
KNOWLEDGE EDITOR achieves high success rate and retain accuracy on fact-checking and question answering tasks.
Using paraphrase supervision during training improves consistency across semantically equivalent inputs.
The updates predicted by KNOWLEDGE EDITOR are sparse and concentrated on attention weight matrices in lower layers, contrasting with gradient-based methods.
KNOWLEDGE EDITOR outperforms fine-tuning and constrained fine-tuning baselines in terms of retaining previous knowledge and generalization to paraphrases.
The hyper-network learns to project gradients to a different direction that preserves other knowledge while editing the target fact.
future_direction: Exploring multiple updates in a loop for editing.
Investigating the mechanism of knowledge encoding in LMs through the lens of editing.
papers.abstract: The factual knowledge acquired during pretraining and stored in the parameters of Language Models (LMs) can be useful in downstream tasks (e.g., question answering or textual inference). However, some facts can be incorrectly induced or become obsolete over time. We present KNOWLEDGEEDITOR, a method which can be used to edit this knowledge and, thus, fix 'bugs' or unexpected predictions without the need for expensive retraining or fine-tuning. Besides being computationally efficient, KNOWLEDGEEDITOR does not require any modifications in LM pretraining (e.g., the use of meta-learning). In our approach, we train a hyper-network with constrained optimization to modify a fact without affecting the rest of the knowledge; the trained hyper-network is then used to predict the weight update at test time. We show KNOWL-EDGEEDITOR's efficacy with two popular architectures and knowledge-intensive tasks: i) a BERT model fine-tuned for fact-checking, and ii) a sequence-to-sequence BART model for question answering. With our method, changing a prediction on the specific wording of a query tends to result in a consistent change in predictions also for its paraphrases. We show that this can be further encouraged by exploiting (e.g., automatically-generated) paraphrases during training. Interestingly, our hyper-network can be regarded as a 'probe' revealing which components need to be changed to manipulate factual knowledge; our analysis shows that the updates tend to be concentrated on a small subset of components. 1 How is Namibia's capital city called? papers.title: Language-Specific Latent Process Hinders Cross-Lingual Performance
papers.research_question: How do language models generalize knowledge to multiple languages, and why do they produce inconsistent outputs across languages?
papers.core_contribution: Larger LLMs tend to reason in language-specific subspaces, hindering cross-lingual consistency and transfer, while smaller models rely on a shared English-aligned semantic space; steering smaller models towards this shared space improves their multilingual performance.
papers.conclusion: The use of shared semantic space facilitates cross-lingual transfer, and inducing processing in this space can improve multilingual reasoning in smaller models.
papers.key_findings:
Larger models are more accurate but less consistent across languages.
Cross-lingual representation similarity predicts knowledge transfer and consistency.
Larger models operate more in language-specific subspaces, while smaller models use a shared English-aligned space.
Cross-lingual activation steering towards English improves performance and consistency in smaller models.
papers.limitation:
The steering method is only tested on multi-choice questions and requires extraction of language-specific activation vectors, which may not generalize to other use cases.
The method may reinforce cultural and linguistic biases towards English.
future_direction: Develop more comprehensive methods to encode knowledge of different languages in the shared semantic space.
Address the limitation of reinforcing English bias in multilingual models.
