With our method, changing a prediction on the specific wording of a query tends to result in a consistent change in predictions also for its paraphrases. We show that this can be further encouraged by exploiting (e.g., automatically-generated) paraphrases during training. Interestingly, our hyper-network can be regarded as a 'probe' revealing which components need to be changed to manipulate factual knowledge; our analysis shows that the updates tend to be concentrated on a small subset of components. 1 How is Namibia's capital city called? papers.title: Language-Specific Latent Process Hinders Cross-Lingual Performance
papers.research_question: How do language models generalize knowledge to multiple languages, and why do they produce inconsistent outputs across languages?
papers.core_contribution: Larger LLMs tend to reason in language-specific subspaces, hindering cross-lingual consistency and transfer, while smaller models rely on a shared English-aligned semantic space; steering smaller models towards this shared space improves their multilingual performance.
papers.conclusion: The use of shared semantic space facilitates cross-lingual transfer, and inducing processing in this space can improve multilingual reasoning in smaller models.
papers.key_findings:
Larger models are more accurate but less consistent across languages.
Cross-lingual representation similarity predicts knowledge transfer and consistency.
Larger models operate more in language-specific subspaces, while smaller models use a shared English-aligned space.
Cross-lingual activation steering towards English improves performance and consistency in smaller models.
papers.limitation:
The steering method is only tested on multi-choice questions and requires extraction of language-specific activation vectors, which may not generalize to other use cases.
The method may reinforce cultural and linguistic biases towards English.
future_direction: Develop more comprehensive methods to encode knowledge of different languages in the shared semantic space.
Address the limitation of reinforcing English bias in multilingual models.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are demonstrably capable of cross-lingual transfer, but can produce inconsistent output when prompted with the same queries written in different languages. To understand how language models are able to generalize knowledge from one language to the others, we measure representation similarity between languages, and apply the logit lens to interpret the implicit steps taken by LLMs to solve multilingual multi-choice reasoning questions. Our analyses reveal LLMs predict inconsistently and are less accurate because they rely on representations that are dissimilar across languages, rather than working in a shared semantic space. While larger models are more multilingual, we show their hidden states are more likely to dissociate from the shared representation compared to smaller models, but are nevertheless more capable of retrieving knowledge embedded across different languages. Finally, we demonstrate that knowledge sharing in small models can be facilitated by steering their latent processing towards the shared semantic space. This improves the models' multilingual reasoning performance, as a result of more knowledge transfer from, and better output consistency with English.

papers.title: Learning to Edit: Aligning LLMs with Knowledge Editing
papers.research_question: How to teach LLMs to dynamically apply updated knowledge to answer queries, rather than relying on memorization.
papers.core_contribution: The LTE framework teaches LLMs to apply updated knowledge through an alignment phase with fine-tuning and an inference phase with retrieval, achieving state-of-the-art performance in knowledge editing.
papers.conclusion: LTE is a novel approach for effective and efficient knowledge editing of LLMs, demonstrating superior performance and robustness.
papers.key_findings:
LTE establishes a new state-of-the-art in knowledge editing performance, surpassing existing methods by over 20 points in portability.
LTE shows robustness in batch and sequential editing with minimal performance deterioration.
LTE has minimal interference on general tasks, maintaining model capabilities across varied domains.
LTE combines fast editing speeds with exceptional performance.
LTE effectively applies updated knowledge through compositional reasoning, as demonstrated in case studies.
papers.limitation:
LTE requires a one-time fine-tuning process, which may be computationally expensive.
Potential issues with retrieval accuracy in the inference phase.
papers.abstract: Knowledge editing techniques, aiming to efficiently modify a minor proportion of knowledge in large language models (LLMs) without negatively impacting performance across other inputs, have garnered widespread attention. However, existing methods predominantly rely on memorizing the updated knowledge, impeding LLMs from effectively combining the new knowledge with their inherent knowledge when answering questions. To this end, we propose a Learning to Edit (LTE) framework, focusing on teaching LLMs to apply updated knowledge into input questions, inspired by the philosophy of "Teach a man to fish." LTE features a two-phase process: (i) the Alignment Phase, which fine-tunes LLMs on a meticulously curated parallel dataset to make reliable, in-scope edits while preserving out-of-scope information and linguistic proficiency; and (ii) the Inference Phase, which employs a retrieval-based mechanism for real-time and mass knowledge editing. By comparing our approach with seven advanced baselines across four popular knowledge editing benchmarks and two LLM architectures, we demonstrate LTE's superiority in knowledge editing performance, robustness in both batch and sequential editing, minimal interference on general tasks, and rapid editing speeds. The data and code are available at https://github.com/YJiangcm/LTE.

papers.title: REACT: Representation Extraction And Controllable Tuning to Overcome Overfitting in LLM Knowledge Editing
papers.research_question: How to overcome overfitting in LLM knowledge editing by precisely and controllably editing knowledge without overfitting to the edit target.
papers.core_contribution: Introduces REACT, a two-phase framework for knowledge editing that extracts a belief-shift vector and applies controllable perturbations to hidden states, reducing overfitting while maintaining balanced editing performance.
papers.conclusion: REACT provides a practical framework for controlled knowledge editing, reducing overfitting and generalizing well, and points towards refining LLM editing without heavy parameter tuning.
papers.key_findings:
REACT achieves balanced performance across reliability, locality, and generality, outperforming baselines by at least 20 percentage points on average.
REACT shows high portability, indicating robust knowledge editing and resilience against overfitting.
REACT significantly reduces overfitting, as evidenced by lower Direct Probability scores and high Editing Overfit Scores on EVOKE.
REACT exhibits balanced calibration in Correct Answer Probability, avoiding overconfident updates.
REACT generalizes well across benchmarks, despite being trained only on COUNTERFACT.
papers.limitation:
Achieving the best possible performance typically requires fine-tuning or retraining on the specific dataset relevant to the task.
Further investigation is required to understand how edits influence broader linguistic abilities, including nuanced semantic understanding and language generation coherence.
papers.abstract: Large language model editing methods frequently suffer from overfitting, wherein factual updates can propagate beyond their intended scope, overemphasizing the edited target even when it's contextually inappropriate. To address this challenge, we introduce REACT (Representation Extraction And Controllable Tuning), a unified two-phase framework designed for precise and controllable knowledge editing. In the initial phase, we utilize tailored stimuli to extract latent factual representations and apply Principal Component Analysis with a simple learnbale linear transformation to compute a directional "belief shift" vector for each instance. In the second phase, we apply controllable perturbations to hidden states using the obtained vector with a magnitude scalar, gated by a pre-trained classifier that permits edits only when contextually necessary. Relevant experiments on EVOKE benchmarks demonstrate that REACT significantly reduces overfitting across nearly all evaluation metrics, and experiments on COUNTERFACT and MQuAKE shows that our method preserves balanced basic editing performance (reliability, locality, and generality) under diverse editing scenarios.

papers.title: History Matters: Temporal Knowledge Editing in Large Language Model
papers.research_question: How can we edit temporal knowledge in large language models to update outdated information while preserving historical knowledge?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces the Temporal Knowledge Editing (TKE) task and the ATOKE benchmark, and proposes the METO framework to enhance existing knowledge editing methods by preserving historical knowledge while learning new knowledge.
papers.conclusion: Temporal Knowledge Editing remains a challenging task, but the METO framework improves existing methods; further community effort is needed.
papers.key_findings:
Existing knowledge editing methods cause catastrophic forgetting of historical knowledge when updating temporal facts.
Relative time questions (e.g., 'previous') are more difficult for edited models than explicit time questions.
Performance degrades with multiple consecutive edits on the same fact.
Extending the time scope of a fact is easier for models than inserting a new object.
The proposed METO framework significantly improves historical knowledge preservation while maintaining effectiveness on new knowledge.
future_direction: Further research on temporal knowledge editing.
papers.abstract: The imperative task of revising or updating the knowledge stored within large language models arises from two distinct sources: intrinsic errors inherent in the model which should be corrected and outdated knowledge due to external shifts in the real world which should be updated. Prevailing efforts in model editing conflate these two distinct categories of edits arising from distinct reasons and directly modify the original knowledge in models into new knowledge. However, we argue that preserving the model's original knowledge remains pertinent. Specifically, if a model's knowledge becomes outdated due to evolving worldly dynamics, it should retain recollection of the historical knowledge while integrating the newfound knowledge. In this work, we introduce the task of Temporal Knowledge Editing (TKE) and establish a benchmark AToKe (Assessment of TempOral Knowledge Editing) to evaluate current model editing methods. We find that while existing model editing methods are effective at making models remember new knowledge, the edited model catastrophically forgets historical knowledge. To address this gap, we propose a simple and general framework termed Multi-Editing with Time Objective (METO) for enhancing existing editing models, which edits both historical and new knowledge concurrently and optimizes the model's prediction for the time of each fact. Our assessments demonstrate that while AToKe is still difficult, METO maintains the effectiveness of learning new knowledge and meanwhile substantially improves the performance of edited models on utilizing historical knowledge.

papers.title: Lost in Multilinguality: Dissecting Cross-lingual Factual Inconsistency in Transformer Language Models
papers.research_question: What are the underlying causes of cross-lingual factual inconsistency in multilingual language models, and how can this inconsistency be mitigated?
papers.core_contribution: The paper identifies that cross-lingual factual inconsistency in multilingual language models arises from failures in the language transition phase in the final layers, and proposes a linear shortcut method that bypasses these layers to improve both prediction accuracy and cross-lingual consistency.
papers.conclusion: Language transition errors are a key cause of cross-lingual inconsistency, and the proposed linear shortcut method effectively mitigates this issue, improving model consistency and accuracy.
papers.key_findings:
Multilingual language models encode factual knowledge in a language-independent concept space through most layers, transitioning to language-specific spaces only in the final layers.
Incorrect predictions in the target language often occur due to failures during the language transition, even when the correct answer is present in the concept space.
The proposed linear shortcut method, which bypasses final-layer computations, enhances prediction accuracy and cross-lingual consistency.
The concept space in LLaMA2 is English-centric, while BLOOM's concept space is more linguistically diverse.
The knowledge recall process in multilingual models involves three stages: relation processing, object extraction in the latent language, and language-specific adaptation.
papers.limitation:
The analysis assumes English as the pivot language, which may limit applicability to language pairs that do not involve English.
The KLAR dataset covers 17 languages but does not fully capture the diversity of world languages.
The shortcut method relies on linear approximation; non-linear approaches might better capture complex transformations.
The study does not explore downstream applications such as multilingual knowledge localization or editing.
future_direction: Expand the investigation to more languages and additional language models to assess broader applicability.
Develop non-linear shortcut methods to better mitigate language transition errors.
papers.abstract: Multilingual language models (MLMs) store factual knowledge across languages but often struggle to provide consistent responses to semantically equivalent prompts in different languages. While previous studies point out this cross-lingual inconsistency issue, the underlying causes remain unexplored. In this work, we use mechanistic interpretability methods to investigate cross-lingual inconsistencies in MLMs. We find that MLMs encode knowledge in a language-independent concept space through most layers, and only transition to language-specific spaces in the final layers. Failures during the language transition often result in incorrect predictions in the target language, even when the answers are correct in other languages. To mitigate this inconsistency issue, we propose a linear shortcut method that bypasses computations in the final layers, enhancing both prediction accuracy and cross-lingual consistency. Our findings shed light on the internal mechanisms of MLMs and provide a lightweight, effective strategy for producing more consistent factual outputs.

papers.title: SAKE: Steering Activations for Knowledge Editing
papers.research_question: How can knowledge editing in large language models be made more robust and generalizable to logical implications and contextual variations?
papers.core_contribution: SAKE introduces a knowledge editing method that models facts as distributions and uses optimal transport to map activations, enabling more robust edits with better generalization to logical implications and contextual robustness.
papers.conclusion: SAKE leverages optimal transport to better capture the distribution of knowledge affected by edits, performing more robust and flexible edits compared to existing methods.
papers.key_findings:
SAKE outperforms weight editing methods like ROME and MEMIT in logical implication metrics such as Compositionality I, II, Subject Aliasing, and Relation Specificity.
SAKE demonstrates superior contextual robustness to doubtful prompts compared to baselines like ROME, ActAdd, and in-context learning.
On traditional KE metrics, SAKE achieves high accuracy and generality, comparable to ROME, with significant improvement in generality due to distribution modeling.
Ablation studies show that SAKE's performance scales with the number of training prompts and that optimal transport mapping provides benefits over simple uniform steering.
papers.limitation:
Relies heavily on the assumption that in-scope distributions can be accurately modeled, and it remains unclear if empirical distributions fully capture all learnable implications.
Does not address reverse relations, a type of logical implication that cannot be easily integrated.
future_direction: Conduct experiments in specialized contexts such as Q&A.
Explore strategies for improving the synthetic generation of source and target distributions, e.g., through automatic differentiation via text-based iterative agent collaborations.
papers.abstract: As Large Langue Models have been shown to memorize real-world facts, the need to update this knowledge in a controlled and efficient manner arises. Designed with these constraints in mind, Knowledge Editing (KE) approaches propose to alter specific facts in pretrained models. However, they have been shown to suffer from several limitations, including their lack of contextual robustness and their failure to generalize to logical implications related to the fact. To overcome these issues, we propose SAKE, a steering activation method that models a fact to be edited as a distribution rather than a single prompt. Leveraging Optimal Transport, SAKE alters the LLM behavior over a whole fact-related distribution, defined as paraphrases and logical implications. Several numerical experiments demonstrate the effectiveness of this method: SAKE is thus able to perform more robust edits than its existing counterparts.

papers.title: Revealing the Deceptiveness of Knowledge Editing: A Mechanistic Analysis of Superficial Editing
papers.research_question: Why do knowledge-edited language models revert to their original knowledge when presented with carefully crafted prompts (attack probes), despite appearing successfully edited according to conventional metrics?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces the concept of superficial editing, provides evaluation datasets and metrics, and identifies two key mechanistic factors: the residual stream at the last subject position in earlier layers and specific attention modules in later layers, showing that specific attention heads and their left singular vectors encode original knowledge and cause superficial editing.
papers.conclusion: Superficial editing is a significant challenge for knowledge editing, and the mechanistic analysis reveals the underlying factors in the residual stream and attention modules, with broader applicability to unlearning tasks.
papers.key_findings:
Existing knowledge editing algorithms achieve near-perfect conventional metrics but are vulnerable to attack probes, exhibiting superficial editing in over 70% of cases for some methods.
The residual stream at the last subject position in earlier layers shows inhibited enrichment of new knowledge and limited accumulation of original knowledge.
Later attention modules cause the Reversal of the Residual Stream (RRS) phenomenon by incorporating original knowledge into the last position, leading to superficial editing.
Specific attention heads in later layers and their left singular vectors are causally responsible for encoding original knowledge and inducing superficial editing.
Similar patterns are observed in superficial unlearning, demonstrating the generality of the findings.
papers.abstract: Knowledge editing, which aims to update the knowledge encoded in language models, can be deceptive. Despite the fact that many existing knowledge editing algorithms achieve near-perfect performance on conventional metrics, the models edited by them are still prone to generating original knowledge. This paper introduces the concept of "superficial editing" to describe this phenomenon. Our comprehensive evaluation reveals that this issue presents a significant challenge to existing algorithms. Through systematic investigation, we identify and validate two key factors contributing to this issue: (1) the residual stream at the last subject position in earlier layers and (2) specific attention modules in later layers. Notably, certain attention heads in later layers, along with specific left singular vectors in their output matrices, encapsulate the original knowledge and exhibit a causal relationship with superficial editing. Furthermore, we extend our analysis to the task of superficial unlearning, where we observe consistent patterns in the behavior of specific attention heads and their corresponding left singular vectors, thereby demonstrating the robustness and broader applicability of our methodology and conclusions. Our code is available here.

papers.title: CaKE: Circuit-aware Editing Enables Generalizable Knowledge Learners
papers.research_question: Why do current knowledge editing methods fail to generalize updated knowledge to multi-hop reasoning tasks, and how can this be improved?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces CaKE, a circuit-aware knowledge editing method that improves the integration of updated knowledge into reasoning circuits, enabling better generalization in multi-hop reasoning tasks.
papers.conclusion: CaKE aligns knowledge editing with the inherent reasoning architectures of LLMs, enabling generalizable multi-hop knowledge editing.
papers.key_findings:
Current knowledge editing methods like ROME and WISE fail in multi-hop reasoning due to misalignment with reasoning circuits.
CaKE outperforms existing methods on multi-hop benchmarks, achieving an average improvement of 20% in accuracy.
CaKE requires only a few curated data samples to integrate knowledge effectively.
CaKE maintains model locality and general ability while editing knowledge.
papers.limitation:
Focuses primarily on factual knowledge and multi-hop reasoning, not other domains like math or long-form reasoning.
Does not deeply investigate fine-grained circuit components like relational information.
Connection between model abilities and training data is underexplored.
future_direction: Investigate knowledge editing in other reasoning domains such as long-form mathematics.
Explore enhancement of knowledge utilization in slow-thinking paradigms like chain-of-thought.
Develop more concise methods for knowledge editing focusing on fine-grained circuit components.
papers.abstract: Knowledge Editing (KE) enables the modification of outdated or incorrect information in large language models (LLMs). While existing KE methods can update isolated facts, they often fail to generalize these updates to multi-hop reasoning tasks that rely on the modified knowledge. Through an analysis of reasoning circuits -- the neural pathways LLMs use for knowledge-based inference, we find that current layer-localized KE approaches (e.g., MEMIT, WISE), which edit only single or a few model layers, inadequately integrate updated knowledge into these reasoning pathways. To address this limitation, we present CaKE (Circuit-aware Knowledge Editing), a novel method that enhances the effective integration of updated knowledge in LLMs. By only leveraging a few curated data samples guided by our circuit-based analysis, CaKE stimulates the model to develop appropriate reasoning circuits for newly incorporated knowledge. Experiments show that CaKE enables more accurate and consistent use of edited knowledge across related reasoning tasks, achieving an average improvement of 20% in multi-hop reasoning accuracy on the MQuAKE dataset while requiring less memory than existing KE methods. We release the code and data in https://github.com/zjunlp/CaKE.

papers.title: MQuAKE: Assessing Knowledge Editing in Language Models via Multi-Hop Questions
papers.research_question: How well do knowledge-editing methods in language models handle multi-hop questions where the answer should change as an entailed consequence of edited facts?
papers.core_contribution: This paper introduces the MQUAKE benchmark for evaluating knowledge editing methods on multi-hop questions and proposes MeLLo, a memory-based approach that outperforms existing methods.
papers.conclusion: The paper presents MQUAKE to assess knowledge editing via multi-hop questions, shows current methods fail, and proposes MeLLo as an effective alternative that works with large LMs.
papers.key_findings:
Current knowledge-editing methods recall edited facts accurately but fail catastrophically on multi-hop questions that require propagating edits to entailed consequences.
MeLLo, a memory-based approach, significantly outperforms existing knowledge editing methods on MQUAKE, especially when scaled to large LLMs like GPT-3.5.
Performance of edited models drops further when injecting more edits at scale.
Chain-of-thought prompting slightly improves multi-hop performance but still shows significant failures in edited models.
MeLLo does not require model weight updates and can be applied to black-box LLMs, offering greater controllability and scalability.
papers.limitation:
Evaluation mainly on GPT-J and Vicuna, leaving efficacy on other LLMs less explored.
MeLLo requires manually defined prompts to drive language models on new tasks.
Multi-hop questions in MQUAKE are generated by ChatGPT rather than being crafted by humans.
future_direction: Evaluate knowledge editing methods on other LLMs
Study how MeLLo works with smaller models such as GPT-2
Evaluate MeLLo on other tasks
Use human-authored questions for MQUAKE
papers.abstract: The information stored in large language models (LLMs) falls out of date quickly, and retraining from scratch is often not an option. This has recently given rise to a range of techniques for injecting new facts through updating model weights. Current evaluation paradigms are extremely limited, mainly validating the recall of edited facts, but changing one fact should cause rippling changes to the model's related beliefs. If we edit the UK Prime Minister to now be Rishi Sunak, then we should get a different answer to Who is married to the British Prime Minister? In this work, we present a benchmark, MQuAKE (Multi-hop Question Answering for Knowledge Editing), comprising multi-hop questions that assess whether edited models correctly answer questions where the answer should change as an entailed consequence of edited facts. While we find that current knowledge-editing approaches can recall edited facts accurately, they fail catastrophically on the constructed multi-hop questions. We thus propose a simple memory-based approach, MeLLo, which stores all edited facts externally while prompting the language model iteratively to generate answers that are consistent with the edited facts. While MQuAKE remains challenging, we show that MeLLo scales well with LLMs (e.g., OpenAI GPT-3.5-turbo) and outperforms previous model editors by a large margin.

papers.title: Stable Knowledge Editing in Large Language Models
papers.research_question: How can we perform stable knowledge editing in large language models, overcoming the instability caused by assumptions of localized and isolated knowledge?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces StableKE, a knowledge editing method based on knowledge augmentation (Semantic Paraphrase Enhancement and Contextual Description Enrichment) rather than knowledge localization, which demonstrates superior stability across edited knowledge, multi-hop knowledge, unrelated knowledge, and general abilities.
papers.conclusion: StableKE is a simple yet effective method for editing knowledge in LLMs, demonstrating that the quality of data used for augmentation is more crucial than the editing structure itself for achieving stable edits.
papers.key_findings:
StableKE outperforms previous knowledge editing methods (e.g., ROME, MEMIT, MEND, SERAC) across four stability dimensions, especially in large-scale batch and sequential editing settings.
The method maintains the model's instruction-following and chain-of-thought (CoT) capabilities after editing.
Increasing the number of semantic paraphrases (Kspe) improves edited knowledge stability, with performance plateauing after a certain point.
StableKE can be effectively applied using different fine-tuning approaches, including full fine-tuning and parameter-efficient methods like LoRA.
The method is also effective for editing knowledge in closed-source models like ChatGPT via their fine-tuning API.
papers.limitation: Despite StableKE exhibiting stability across various knowledge editing settings, its overall performance exhibits a downward trend in a sequential editing setting.
papers.abstract: Efficient knowledge editing of large language models is crucial for replacing obsolete information or incorporating specialized knowledge on a large scale. However, previous methods implicitly assume that knowledge is localized and isolated within the model, an assumption that oversimplifies the interconnected nature of model knowledge. The premise of localization results in an incomplete knowledge editing, whereas an isolated assumption may impair both other knowledge and general abilities. It introduces instability to the performance of the knowledge editing method. To transcend these assumptions, we introduce StableKE, a method adopts a novel perspective based on knowledge augmentation rather than knowledge localization. To overcome the expense of human labeling, StableKE integrates two automated knowledge augmentation strategies: Semantic Paraphrase Enhancement strategy, which diversifies knowledge descriptions to facilitate the teaching of new information to the model, and Contextual Description Enrichment strategy, expanding the surrounding knowledge to prevent the forgetting of related information. StableKE surpasses other knowledge editing methods, demonstrating stability both edited knowledge and multi-hop knowledge, while also preserving unrelated knowledge and general abilities. Moreover, StableKE can edit knowledge on ChatGPT.

papers.title: How multilingual is Multilingual BERT?
papers.research_question: Why is Multilingual BERT (M-BERT) effective at zero-shot cross-lingual model transfer?
papers.core_contribution: M-BERT learns multilingual representations from monolingual corpora, enabling zero-shot cross-lingual transfer, but transfer effectiveness depends on typological similarity and script consistency.
papers.conclusion: M-BERT's cross-lingual transfer ability is due to multilingual representations learned from monolingual data, but for full effectiveness across all language pairs, explicit multilingual training objectives are needed.
papers.key_findings:
M-BERT can perform cross-lingual transfer even between languages with different scripts, indicating deep multilingual representations beyond vocabulary memorization.
Transfer performance is higher for typologically similar languages, suggesting that the model maps structures but does not learn systematic transformations for different word orders.
M-BERT generalizes to code-switched text when trained on monolingual data, showing its multilingual representation capability.
The model struggles with transliterated text, indicating limitations in handling non-standard scripts without explicit training.
The feature space of M-BERT allows for finding translation pairs through vector arithmetic, demonstrating a shared multilingual subspace.
papers.limitation:
Transfer is less accurate for languages with different word orders, such as English and Japanese.
M-BERT does not generalize well to transliterated text without explicit transliteration signals.
future_direction: Incorporate explicit multilingual training objectives to improve transfer to typologically divergent and transliterated targets.
papers.abstract: In this paper, we show that Multilingual BERT (M-BERT), released by Devlin et al. (2018) as a single language model pre-trained from monolingual corpora in 104 languages, is surprisingly good at zero-shot cross-lingual model transfer, in which task-specific annotations in one language are used to fine-tune the model for evaluation in another language. To understand why, we present a large number of probing experiments, showing that transfer is possible even to languages in different scripts, that transfer works best between typologically similar languages, that monolingual corpora can train models for code-switching, and that the model can find translation pairs. From these results, we can conclude that M-BERT does create multilingual representations, but that these representations exhibit systematic deficiencies affecting certain language pairs.

papers.title: Unveiling the Pitfalls of Knowledge Editing for Large Language Models
papers.research_question: Does knowledge editing for LLMs introduce irreversible unforeseen side effects, such as knowledge conflict and knowledge distortion?
papers.core_contribution: This paper investigates pitfalls of knowledge editing in LLMs, identifying knowledge conflict and knowledge distortion as major issues, and introduces benchmark datasets and metrics to evaluate these pitfalls.
papers.conclusion: Knowledge editing might inadvertently cast a shadow of unintended consequences on LLMs, such as knowledge conflict and distortion, which warrant attention and efforts for future works.
papers.key_findings:
Knowledge conflict arises when editing groups of facts that logically clash, magnifying inherent inconsistencies in LLMs.
Knowledge distortion occurs when editing factual knowledge irrevocably warps the innate knowledge structure of LLMs.
Existing knowledge editing methods (FT, MEND, ROME, MEMIT) all suffer from knowledge conflict and distortion issues.
The proposed Multi-Label Edit (MLE) method can alleviate knowledge distortion by editing multiple correct labels simultaneously.
The paper provides a unified view of knowledge conflict scenarios (Coverage, Reverse, Composite) based on editing scope.
papers.abstract: As the cost associated with fine-tuning Large Language Models (LLMs) continues to rise, recent research efforts have pivoted towards developing methodologies to edit implicit knowledge embedded within LLMs. Yet, there's still a dark cloud lingering overhead -- will knowledge editing trigger butterfly effect? since it is still unclear whether knowledge editing might introduce side effects that pose potential risks or not. This paper pioneers the investigation into the potential pitfalls associated with knowledge editing for LLMs. To achieve this, we introduce new benchmark datasets and propose innovative evaluation metrics. Our results underline two pivotal concerns: (1) Knowledge Conflict: Editing groups of facts that logically clash can magnify the inherent inconsistencies in LLMs-a facet neglected by previous methods. (2) Knowledge Distortion: Altering parameters with the aim of editing factual knowledge can irrevocably warp the innate knowledge structure of LLMs. Experimental results vividly demonstrate that knowledge editing might inadvertently cast a shadow of unintended consequences on LLMs, which warrant attention and efforts for future works. Code and data are available at https://github.com/zjunlp/PitfallsKnowledgeEditing.

papers.title: Conflict-Resolving and Sharpness-Aware Minimization for Generalized Knowledge Editing with Multiple Updates
papers.research_question: How to effectively update knowledge in large language models with multiple updates while improving generalization, stability, and resolving conflicts with prior knowledge?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes CORSA, a training framework for knowledge editing that uses Sharpness-Aware Minimization and Direct Preference Optimization to improve generalization, stability across multiple updates, and conflict resolution between new and old knowledge.
papers.conclusion: CORSA is a holistic framework for knowledge updating that addresses generalization, stability, and conflict resolution, demonstrating strong performance across factual and code domains while scaling efficiently.
papers.key_findings:
CORSA outperforms baselines like LoRA and MEMIT in generalization by an average of 12.42% and 10% respectively on factual benchmarks.
CORSA reduces catastrophic forgetting by 27.82% compared to LoRA in multi-update settings.
The method generalizes to the code domain, outperforming the strongest baseline by 5.48% Pass@5 in update efficacy.
CORSA maintains model specificity (general capabilities) close to the base model, with only marginal drops.
The framework scales effectively to larger models (e.g., Qwen3-14B) and supports adapter merging with minimal interference.
papers.limitation:
Current updating methods, including CORSA, are imperfect and may introduce failures and unintended side effects such as hallucinations.
The method increases training time by approximately 1.8-2.5x compared to standard LoRA due to the need for two forward-backward passes per step.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) rely on internal knowledge to solve many downstream tasks, making it crucial to keep them up to date. Since full retraining is expensive, prior work has explored efficient alternatives such as model editing and parameter-efficient fine-tuning. However, these approaches often break down in practice due to poor generalization across inputs, limited stability, and knowledge conflict. To address these limitations, we propose the CoRSA (Conflict-Resolving and Sharpness-Aware Minimization) training framework, a parameter-efficient, holistic approach for knowledge editing with multiple updates. CoRSA tackles multiple challenges simultaneously: it improves generalization to different input forms and enhances stability across multiple updates by minimizing loss curvature, and resolves conflicts by maximizing the margin between new and prior knowledge. Across three widely used fact editing benchmarks, CoRSA achieves significant gains in generalization, outperforming baselines with average absolute improvements of 12.42% over LoRA and 10% over model editing methods. With multiple updates, it maintains high update efficacy while reducing catastrophic forgetting by 27.82% compared to LoRA. CoRSA also generalizes to the code domain, outperforming the strongest baseline by 5.48% Pass@5 in update efficacy.

papers.title: First Align, then Predict: Understanding the Cross-Lingual Ability of Multilingual BERT
papers.research_question: What parts of the model and what mechanisms support zero-shot cross-lingual transfer in multilingual BERT?
papers.core_contribution: mBERT operates as the stacking of two modules: a multilingual encoder in the lower layers critical for cross-lingual transfer, and a task-specific, language-agnostic predictor in the upper layers that has little importance for transfer.
papers.conclusion: mBERT is constructed from a multilingual encoder in the lower layers that aligns representations across languages and is critical for cross-language transfer, and a task-specific, language-agnostic predictor in the upper layers that has little effect on transfer.
papers.key_findings:
Lower layers of mBERT are critical for cross-lingual transfer, while upper layers are task-specific and language-agnostic.
Cross-lingual similarity (CKA) between representations of source and target languages is highest in the middle layers and strongly correlates with cross-lingual performance.
Randomly initializing lower layers harms cross-lingual performance but not same-language performance, indicating their specific role in cross-lingual alignment.
The cross-lingual alignment learned during pretraining is preserved after fine-tuning.
This mechanism suggests mBERT reproduces the standard cross-lingual pipeline without explicit supervision.
future_direction: Using the findings to design better multilingual pre-training processes.
Inspecting the mismatch with Singh et al. (2019) who found no language alignment across layers for Natural Language Inference.
papers.abstract: Multilingual pretrained language models have demonstrated remarkable zero-shot crosslingual transfer capabilities. Such transfer emerges by fine-tuning on a task of interest in one language and evaluating on a distinct language, not seen during the fine-tuning. Despite promising results, we still lack a proper understanding of the source of this transfer. Using a novel layer ablation technique and analyses of the model's internal representations, we show that multilingual BERT, a popular multilingual language model, can be viewed as the stacking of two sub-networks: a multilingual encoder followed by a taskspecific language-agnostic predictor. While the encoder is crucial for cross-lingual transfer and remains mostly unchanged during finetuning, the task predictor has little importance on the transfer and can be reinitialized during fine-tuning. We present extensive experiments with three distinct tasks, seventeen typologically diverse languages and multiple domains to support our hypothesis.

papers.title: Aligning Language Models with Real-time Knowledge Editing
papers.research_question: How can we efficiently edit outdated knowledge in language models in real-time, and how can we evaluate such editing in a dynamic, real-world setting?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces CRAFT, a real-time knowledge editing dataset, and KEDAS, a method for real-time knowledge editing alignment that achieves balanced performance in edit success, locality, and portability.
papers.conclusion: The work introduces CRAFT and KEDAS to advance real-time knowledge editing and hopes to shift the focus from static update to dynamic evolution.
papers.key_findings:
CRAFT dataset has nearly zero exposure rate, making it a challenging and fair benchmark for real-time knowledge editing.
Existing knowledge editing methods show limitations on CRAFT, struggling to achieve balanced performance.
KEDAS achieves nearly 100% edit success, 100% locality on common-sense, and high portability on CRAFT.
KEDAS outperforms previous methods on both CRAFT and traditional knowledge editing datasets.
The diverse edit augmentation and self-adaptive inference in KEDAS are key to its balanced performance.
papers.limitation:
CRAFT is limited to Chinese language and domains of statistics and finance.
Composite reasoning portability in CRAFT is only 2-hop.
Only a limited set of existing methods is evaluated due to resources and compatibility.
The performance of KEDAS heavily depends on the filter, which may not be sufficiently robust.
papers.abstract: Knowledge editing aims to modify outdated knowledge in large language models (LLMs) efficiently while retaining their original capabilities. Mainstream benchmarks for knowledge editing are predominantly static and fail to keep in pace with the evolving real-world knowledge. In this work, we introduce CRAFT, an ever-evolving real-world benchmark for knowledge editing. It features well-designed paired edits for composite reasoning, and evaluates models on alias portability as well as temporal and common-sense locality, making it a challenging knowledge editing benchmark on which previous knowledge editing methods hardly achieve balanced performance. Towards flexible real-time editing, we propose KEDAS, a novel paradigm of knowledge editing alignment featuring diverse edit augmentation and self-adaptive post-alignment inference, which exhibits significant performance gain on CRAFT compared to previous methods. All of our code and data are available at https://anonymous.4open.science/r/CRAFT-KEDAS.

papers.title: Model Editing at Scale leads to Gradual and Catastrophic Forgetting
papers.research_question: How do model editing methods scale with multiple sequential edits, and what are their limitations in terms of forgetting and downstream performance?
papers.core_contribution: Model editing methods like ROME and MEMIT suffer from gradual and catastrophic forgetting when applied sequentially at scale, limiting their practical utility.
papers.conclusion: Current model editing methods have scalability issues due to gradual and catastrophic forgetting, and improved evaluation frameworks are needed for practical use.
papers.key_findings:
Sequential editing leads to gradual forgetting of previously edited facts and degradation in downstream task performance.
After a point, catastrophic forgetting occurs, where the model abruptly loses all coherence and function.
Edits made by ROME and MEMIT are not fully localized and bleed into other facts.
MEMIT has a longer gradual forgetting phase and forgets fewer facts compared to ROME.
The source of forgetting is the increasing distance between edited layer weights and original weights, leading to incompatibility.
papers.limitation:
The study is limited to models of size 1.5B and 6B parameters, and larger models might respond differently.
Batch edits and combining multiple batches sequentially are not evaluated, which are natural extensions.
future_direction: Evaluate model editing on larger model sizes
Investigate batch edits with increasing batch sizes
Study combining multiple batches of edits sequentially
papers.abstract: Editing knowledge in large language models is an attractive capability to have which allows us to correct incorrectly learnt facts during pre-training, as well as update the model with an ever-growing list of new facts. While existing model editing techniques have shown promise, they are usually evaluated using metrics for reliability, specificity and generalization over one or few edits. We argue that for model editing to have practical utility, we must be able to make multiple edits to the same model. With this in mind, we evaluate the current model editing methods at scale, focusing on two state of the art methods: ROME and MEMIT. We find that as the model is edited sequentially with multiple facts, it continually forgets previously edited facts and the ability to perform downstream tasks. This forgetting happens in two phases -- an initial gradual but progressive forgetting phase followed by abrupt or catastrophic forgetting phase. Both gradual and catastrophic forgetting limit the usefulness of model editing methods at scale -- the former making model editing less effective as multiple edits are made to the model while the latter caps the scalability of such model editing methods. Our analysis also highlights other key limitations of ROME and MEMIT at scale. With our work, we push for the development and evaluation of model editing methods keeping scalability in mind.

papers.title: How do languages influence each other? Studying cross-lingual data sharing during LM fine-tuning
papers.research_question: To what extent, and under which conditions, do multilingual language models rely on data from multiple languages during fine-tuning?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces the use of Training Data Attribution (TDA) methods, specifically TracIn, to study cross-lingual sharing at the data level in multilingual language models, finding that models rely on data from multiple languages during fine-tuning and this reliance increases as fine-tuning progresses.
papers.conclusion: The study shows that languages largely influence one another cross-lingually under various conditions, with cross-lingual sharing increasing during fine-tuning and languages playing both reinforcing and complementary roles.
papers.key_findings:
MLMs rely on data from multiple languages during fine-tuning and this reliance increases as fine-tuning progresses.
Training samples from other languages can both reinforce and complement the knowledge acquired from data of the test language itself.
The model exhibits different cross-lingual behaviour in zero-shot testing compared to when the test language is seen during fine-tuning.
Even with data imbalances, the model largely benefits from cross-lingual sharing.
For parallel datasets, cross-lingual sharing is high, and for non-parallel datasets, it is still observed but to a lesser extent.
papers.limitation:
Computational expense limited the study to 125 test samples.
The method is restricted to relatively easy classification tasks and not generation or sequence labeling tasks.
The analysis focuses on the fine-tuning stage and does not disentangle pre-training effects.
future_direction: Extending influence function methods to sequence tagging tasks for more fine-grained analysis.
Studying the emergence of cross-lingual abilities during pre-training.
Inspiring future work on studying sharing mechanisms within multi-task and multi-modal models.
papers.abstract: Multilingual large language models (MLLMs) are jointly trained on data from many different languages such that representation of individual languages can benefit from other languages' data. Impressive performance on zero-shot cross-lingual transfer shows that these models are capable of exploiting data from other languages. Yet, it remains unclear to what extent, and under which conditions, languages rely on each other's data. In this study, we use TracIn (Pruthi et al., 2020), a training data attribution (TDA) method, to retrieve the most influential training samples seen during multilingual fine-tuning for a particular test language. This allows us to analyse cross-lingual sharing mechanisms of MLLMs from a new perspective. While previous work studied cross-lingual sharing at the level of model parameters, we present the first approach to study cross-lingual sharing at the data level. We find that MLLMs rely on data from multiple languages from the early stages of fine-tuning and that this reliance gradually increases as fine-tuning progresses. We further study how different fine-tuning languages influence model performance on a given test language and find that they can both reinforce and complement the knowledge acquired from data of the test language itself.

papers.title: ACE: Attribution-Controlled Knowledge Editing for Multi-hop Factual Recall
papers.research_question: How can knowledge editing for multi-hop factual recall in LLMs be improved by understanding and leveraging internal neuron-level mechanisms?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces ACE, a knowledge editing framework that uses neuron-level attribution to identify and edit query-value pathways, improving multi-hop factual recall.
papers.conclusion: ACE provides a mechanistically grounded solution for multi-hop knowledge editing and establishes a new pathway for advancing KE capabilities based on understanding internal reasoning mechanisms.
papers.key_findings:
LLMs store semantically analogous knowledge in structurally similar transformer components, with query and value neurons for specific knowledge types exhibiting consistent localization patterns.
During multi-hop reasoning, implicit subjects function as query neurons that sequentially activate corresponding value neurons across layers to accumulate information toward the final answer.
ACE outperforms state-of-the-art KE methods by 9.44% on GPT-J and 37.46% on Qwen3-8B in multi-hop accuracy.
Ablating query layers causes a 16.51% performance drop, while omitting value layers leads to a 40.45% decrease, demonstrating the necessity of both components.
GPT-J maintains fixed layer separation for query and value neurons, while Qwen3-8B exhibits dynamic, domain-specific alignment.
papers.limitation:
Focuses on FFN layers and does not edit attention heads, which may limit editability for some knowledge types.
Attribution mechanism relies on first-order Taylor approximation, potentially missing higher-order interactions.
Requires forward passes to compute importance scores, adding computational overhead.
future_direction: Integrating attention head editing into the ACE framework.
Developing more efficient attribution algorithms to reduce computational overhead.
Extending ACE to other model architectures and tasks beyond factual recall.
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) require efficient knowledge editing (KE) to update factual information, yet existing methods exhibit significant performance decay in multi-hop factual recall. This failure is particularly acute when edits involve intermediate implicit subjects within reasoning chains. Through causal analysis, we reveal that this limitation stems from an oversight of how chained knowledge is dynamically represented and utilized at the neuron level. We discover that during multi hop reasoning, implicit subjects function as query neurons, which sequentially activate corresponding value neurons across transformer layers to accumulate information toward the final answer, a dynamic prior KE work has overlooked. Guided by this insight, we propose ACE: Attribution-Controlled Knowledge Editing for Multi-hop Factual Recall, a framework that leverages neuron-level attribution to identify and edit these critical query-value (Q-V) pathways. ACE provides a mechanistically grounded solution for multi-hop KE, empirically outperforming state-of-the-art methods by 9.44% on GPT-J and 37.46% on Qwen3-8B. Our analysis further reveals more fine-grained activation patterns in Qwen3 and demonstrates that the semantic interpretability of value neurons is orchestrated by query-driven accumulation. These findings establish a new pathway for advancing KE capabilities based on the principled understanding of internal reasoning mechanisms.

papers.title: Editing Conceptual Knowledge for Large Language Models
papers.research_question: Whether LLMs can modify conceptual knowledge and how existing editing methods perform on this task.
papers.core_contribution: Introduces ConceptEdit, a benchmark for conceptual knowledge editing in LLMs, and evaluates existing editing methods, showing they can edit concepts but often distort instance-level knowledge.
papers.conclusion: The paper pioneers conceptual knowledge editing for LLMs, providing a benchmark and evaluation metrics, and finds that current methods have limitations in preserving instance-level knowledge after concept edits.
papers.key_findings:
Existing knowledge editing methods (FT, ROME, MEMIT, PROMPT) achieve high reliability in modifying concept-level definitions but perform poorly on instance change metrics.
The new Concept Consistency metric reveals a gap between token-level reliability and semantic similarity of generated definitions.
Conceptual knowledge editing is more effective when concepts are from the same superclass (intra module) compared to different superclasses (inter module).
Causal tracing shows that conceptual knowledge in LLMs is associated with attention mechanisms in early layers, differing from instantial knowledge storage.
papers.limitation:
The scope is confined to a select group of LLMs, and the findings may not generalize to all models.
The analysis of how LLMs learn and represent concepts is cursory and requires more comprehensive study.
papers.abstract: Recently, there has been a growing interest in knowledge editing for Large Language Models (LLMs). Current approaches and evaluations merely explore the instance-level editing, while whether LLMs possess the capability to modify concepts remains unclear. This paper pioneers the investigation of editing conceptual knowledge for LLMs, by constructing a novel benchmark dataset ConceptEdit and establishing a suite of new metrics for evaluation. The experimental results reveal that, although existing editing methods can efficiently modify concept-level definition to some extent, they also have the potential to distort the related instantial knowledge in LLMs, leading to poor performance. We anticipate this can inspire further progress in better understanding LLMs. Our project homepage is available at https://zjunlp.github.io/project/ConceptEdit.

papers.title: Knowledge Editing through Chain-of-Thought
papers.research_question: How can we improve in-context knowledge editing to be more generalizable and stable across diverse tasks without retraining?
papers.core_contribution: The paper proposes EditCoT, a novel knowledge editing framework that updates LLMs by iteratively editing their chain-of-thought, achieving state-of-the-art performance and better generalization across tasks without retraining.
papers.conclusion: EditCoT is an effective and generalizable framework for knowledge editing that updates LLMs through chain-of-thought, outperforming existing methods.
papers.key_findings:
EditCoT achieves top performance on 6 out of 8 results and second-best on 2 out of 8 results in MQuAKE-3k-CF and DUNE.
EditCoT shows better robustness and locality compared to other in-context editing methods.
EditCoT is effective in vertical domains (e.g., legal) and with black-box models (e.g., GPT-4o).
EditCoT's conflict detection mechanism is crucial for correcting reasoning chains.
papers.limitation:
Errors can occur due to suboptimal retriever performance and conflict detection, leading to unnecessary edits.
The method relies on the original LLM's reasoning capabilities, and errors in the original CoT can prevent editing.
papers.abstract: Knowledge Editing is a technique that updates large language models (LLMs) with new information to maintain their world knowledge. This approach avoids the need to rebuild the model from scratch, thereby addressing the high costs associated with frequent retraining. Among these, the in-context editing paradigm stands out for its effectiveness in integrating new knowledge while preserving the model's original capabilities. Despite its potential, existing in-context knowledge editing methods are often task-specific, focusing primarily on multi-hop QA tasks using structured knowledge triples. Moreover, their reliance on few-shot prompting for task decomposition makes them unstable and less effective in generalizing across diverse tasks. In response to these limitations, we propose EditCoT, a novel knowledge editing framework that flexibly and efficiently updates LLMs across various tasks without retraining. EditCoT works by generating a chain-of-thought (CoT) for a given input and then iteratively refining this CoT process using a CoT editor based on updated knowledge. We evaluate EditCoT across a diverse range of benchmarks, covering multiple languages and tasks. The results demonstrate that our approach achieves state-of-the-art performance while offering superior generalization, effectiveness, and stability compared to existing methods, marking a significant advancement in the field of knowledge updating. The code and data of EditCoT are available at: https://github.com/bebr2/EditCoT .

papers.title: SetKE: Knowledge Editing for Knowledge Elements Overlap
papers.research_question: How to effectively edit knowledge in large language models when there is overlap in knowledge elements, which causes conflicts and performance degradation in current methods?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes SetKE, a knowledge editing method that uses bipartite matching to edit sets of triplets simultaneously, addressing the knowledge element overlap problem, and introduces the EDIT SET dataset for evaluation.
papers.conclusion: SetKE leverages bipartite matching to optimize object set editing, effectively resolving editing conflicts and improving accuracy, and experimental results confirm its superiority over existing methods.
papers.key_findings:
KEO is prevalent in existing KE datasets and causes performance degradation in current knowledge editing methods.
SetKE outperforms existing methods in KEO scenarios on mainstream LLMs.
The bipartite matching constraint in SetKE helps mitigate knowledge overwriting issues.
Editing performance degrades as the number of overlap triplets increases.
SetKE effectively edits knowledge sets without additional parameters.
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) excel in tasks such as retrieval and question answering but require updates to incorporate new knowledge and reduce inaccuracies and hallucinations. Traditional updating methods, like fine-tuning and incremental learning, face challenges such as overfitting and high computational costs. Knowledge Editing (KE) provides a promising alternative but often overlooks the Knowledge Element Overlap (KEO) phenomenon, where multiple triplets share common elements, leading to editing conflicts. We identify the prevalence of KEO in existing KE datasets and show its significant impact on current KE methods, causing performance degradation in handling such triplets. To address this, we propose a new formulation, Knowledge Set Editing (KSE), and introduce SetKE, a method that edits sets of triplets simultaneously. Experimental results demonstrate that SetKE outperforms existing methods in KEO scenarios on mainstream LLMs. Additionally, we introduce EditSet, a dataset containing KEO triplets, providing a comprehensive benchmark.

papers.title: Knowledge Editing with Subspace-Aware Key-Value Mappings
papers.research_question: How can we efficiently correct factual errors in language models by constraining edits to subspaces of critical features to reduce unintended perturbations?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes SUIT, a knowledge editing method that constrains edits to subspaces of critical features, reducing unintended perturbations and improving knowledge preservation while maintaining high editing performance.
papers.conclusion: SUIT successfully identifies edit-critical subspaces and enables precise, low-perturbation knowledge editing, establishing subspace identification as a key principle for reliable model editing.
papers.key_findings:
SUIT outperforms strong baselines (e.g., AlphaEdit) in specificity (knowledge preservation) while maintaining high editing efficacy and generalization.
SUIT reduces perturbation at the entity's last token position, where attribute information is predominantly enriched.
The subspaces identified by SUIT (entity-specific and attribute-critical) are more critical for editing than their complements.
SUIT maintains general model capabilities (fluency, consistency, and performance on general benchmarks) after extensive sequential editing.
papers.abstract: Knowledge editing aims to efficiently correct factual errors in Language Models (LMs). The popular locate-then-edit approach modifies an MLP layer by finding an optimal mapping between its input vector (key) and output vector (value) that leads to the expression of the edited knowledge. However, existing methods without any constraints on the key and value vectors cause significant perturbations to the edited model. To address this, we propose Subspace Knowledge Edit (SUIT), a method that identifies and modifies only the subspace of critical features relevant to the edit. Our empirical results on LLaMA-3-8B, GPT-J-6B, and Qwen2.5-7B models show that SUIT dramatically improves knowledge preservation over strong baselines while maintaining high edit efficacy. This effectiveness confirms that SUIT successfully identifies the critical subspace for the edit. Further analyses provide additional validation for our approach. The source code and data will be released to the public upon publication of the paper.

papers.title: AKEW: Assessing Knowledge Editing in the Wild
papers.research_question: How do current knowledge-editing methods perform in practice, particularly when editing with unstructured texts and real-world knowledge updates?
papers.core_contribution: The paper proposes AKEW, a new benchmark for knowledge editing that evaluates methods on structured facts, unstructured texts, and extracted triplets, revealing a significant performance gap between current methods and practical scenarios.
papers.conclusion: Current knowledge-editing methods commonly struggle with unstructured facts, verifying the challenging nature of practical knowledge editing and highlighting the necessity for more research in this area.
papers.key_findings:
Unstructured facts pose more challenges for knowledge editing than structured facts, leading to significant performance declines.
Extracted triplets can help some methods (FT, LoRA) and enable others (ROME, MEMIT) to handle unstructured facts, but performance remains far below that with structured facts.
Real-world knowledge updates (WIKIUPDATE) are more difficult for knowledge editing than counterfactual updates.
In-context learning methods (IKE, MeLLo) perform relatively better on unstructured facts by converting editing into a retrieval-augmented generation task, but still have limitations.
Error analysis shows that for locate-then-edit methods, most failures with extracted triplets are due to editing errors (78%) rather than extraction errors (22%).
future_direction: Enhance locate-then-edit methods to edit with multiple related facts at once.
Improve the retrieval and reasoning processes of in-context learning methods to handle complex unstructured facts.
papers.abstract: Knowledge editing injects knowledge updates into language models to keep them correct and up-to-date. However, its current evaluations deviate significantly from practice: their knowledge updates solely consist of structured facts derived from meticulously crafted datasets, instead of practical sources -- unstructured texts like news articles, and they often overlook practical real-world knowledge updates. To address these issues, in this paper we propose AKEW (Assessing Knowledge Editing in the Wild), a new practical benchmark for knowledge editing. AKEW fully covers three editing settings of knowledge updates: structured facts, unstructured texts as facts, and extracted triplets. It further introduces new datasets featuring both counterfactual and real-world knowledge updates. Through extensive experiments, we demonstrate the considerable gap between state-of-the-art knowledge-editing methods and practical scenarios. Our analyses further highlight key insights to motivate future research for practical knowledge editing.

papers.title: One Mind, Many Tongues: A Deep Dive into Language-Agnostic Knowledge Neurons in Large Language Models
papers.research_question: How can we accurately localize language-agnostic knowledge neurons in large language models, considering uncertainty across queries and languages?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces MATRICE, a method for localizing language-agnostic knowledge neurons by quantifying uncertainty across queries and languages, and constructs the RML-LAMA benchmark. It demonstrates these neurons' roles in cross-lingual editing, knowledge enhancement, and injection.
papers.conclusion: The proposed MATRICE method accurately localizes language-agnostic knowledge neurons, and these neurons are shown to be conducive to cross-lingual knowledge editing, enhancement, and injection.
papers.key_findings:
A significant proportion of language-agnostic knowledge neurons are distributed in the last few layers of LLMs.
Manipulating (suppressing/enhancing) language-agnostic knowledge neurons significantly affects knowledge expression across languages.
A single edit on language-agnostic knowledge neurons can simultaneously modify corresponding knowledge in all languages (cross-lingual editing).
Amplifying the activation of language-agnostic knowledge neurons improves prediction performance in low-resource languages.
Fine-tuning only parameters associated with language-agnostic knowledge neurons helps LLMs learn new knowledge while alleviating forgetting of old knowledge.
papers.limitation: The approach is based on knowledge neuron theory and focuses on factual knowledge, not yet extended to other types like commonsense or event knowledge.
future_direction: Extend the approach to investigate other types of knowledge, such as commonsense knowledge and event knowledge.
Adapt the method to new theoretical frameworks as the theory of knowledge neurons evolves.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have learned vast amounts of factual knowledge through self-supervised pre-training on large-scale corpora. Meanwhile, LLMs have also demonstrated excellent multilingual capabilities, which can express the learned knowledge in multiple languages. However, the knowledge storage mechanism in LLMs still remains mysterious. Some researchers attempt to demystify the factual knowledge in LLMs from the perspective of knowledge neurons, and subsequently discover language-agnostic knowledge neurons that store factual knowledge in a form that transcends language barriers. However, the preliminary finding suffers from two limitations: 1) High Uncertainty in Localization Results. Existing study only uses a prompt-based probe to localize knowledge neurons for each fact, while LLMs cannot provide consistent answers for semantically equivalent queries. Thus, it leads to inaccurate localization results with high uncertainty. 2) Lack of Analysis in More Languages. The study only analyzes language-agnostic knowledge neurons on English and Chinese data, without exploring more language families and languages. Naturally, it limits the generalizability of the findings. To address aforementioned problems, we first construct a new benchmark called Rephrased Multilingual LAMA (RML-LAMA), which contains high-quality cloze-style multilingual parallel queries for each fact. Then, we propose a novel method named Multilingual Integrated Gradients with Uncertainty Estimation (MATRICE), which quantifies the uncertainty across queries and languages during knowledge localization. Extensive experiments show that our method can accurately localize language-agnostic knowledge neurons. We also further investigate the role of language-agnostic knowledge neurons in cross-lingual knowledge editing, knowledge enhancement and new knowledge injection.

papers.title: Rethinking Cross-lingual Alignment: Balancing Transfer and Cultural Erasure in Multilingual LLMs
papers.research_question: What is the trade-off between knowledge transfer and cultural localization in cross-lingual alignment, and how can we design alignment techniques to balance this trade-off?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces a holistic evaluation framework (transfer-localization plane) to measure the trade-off between knowledge transfer and cultural erasure in cross-lingual alignment, and proposes a novel inference-time method (Surgical Steering) that disentangles universal and localized steering at different layers to better balance the two objectives.
papers.conclusion: Cultural knowledge is suppressed but partially recoverable through targeted steering; however, some cultural nuances are irretrievably lost, highlighting a persistent and perhaps unavoidable cost of cross-lingual alignment.
papers.key_findings:
Current cross-lingual alignment methods consistently improve factual transfer at the direct cost of cultural localization across all six languages studied.
Universal factual transfer and culturally-specific knowledge are optimally steerable at different model layers (transfer in middle layers, localization in deeper layers).
Surgical Steering, which applies English steering at a middle layer and localization steering at a deeper layer, achieves a better balance between transfer and localization than applying either alone.
Cultural knowledge is not permanently erased by alignment but is suppressed and can be partially recovered through targeted, layer-specific interventions.
The fundamental trade-off between transfer and localization persists, indicating that some cultural nuances are irretrievably lost during the alignment process.
papers.limitation:
The fundamental trade-off persists; models with stronger alignment are less responsive to steering, indicating that some cultural nuances are irrevocably lost during the alignment process.
English bias is not completely removed even with steering; the post-trained CLA models never fully return to the point of the unaligned baseline.
papers.abstract: Cross-lingual alignment (CLA) aims to align multilingual representations, enabling Large Language Models (LLMs) to seamlessly transfer knowledge across languages. While intuitive, we hypothesize, this pursuit of representational convergence can inadvertently cause "cultural erasure", the functional loss of providing culturally-situated responses that should diverge based on the query language. In this work, we systematically analyze this trade-off by introducing a holistic evaluation framework, the transfer-localization plane, which quantifies both desirable knowledge transfer and undesirable cultural erasure. Using this framework, we re-evaluate recent CLA approaches and find that they consistently improve factual transfer at the direct cost of cultural localization across all six languages studied. Our investigation into the internal representations of these models reveals a key insight: universal factual transfer and culturally-specific knowledge are optimally steerable at different model layers. Based on this finding, we propose Surgical Steering, a novel inference-time method that disentangles these two objectives. By applying targeted activation steering to distinct layers, our approach achieves a better balance between the two competing dimensions, effectively overcoming the limitations of current alignment techniques.

papers.title: Knowledge Editing for Large Language Models: A Survey
papers.research_question: How can we efficiently and precisely update knowledge in large language models without negatively affecting other pre-trained knowledge?
papers.core_contribution: This survey provides a comprehensive and in-depth overview of knowledge-based model editing (KME) for large language models, including a novel categorization of methods, an analysis of their strengths and limitations, and a discussion of future research directions.
papers.conclusion: Knowledge editing is a crucial and rapidly evolving field for efficiently updating large language models. This survey synthesizes current progress, highlights key challenges, and outlines promising directions for future research to advance the practicality and reliability of KME techniques.
papers.key_findings:
KME methods can be categorized into three main strategies: external memorization, global optimization, and local modification.
Locality (preserving unrelated knowledge) and generality (applying edits to related inputs) are two crucial properties for effective knowledge editing.
Existing KME methods face challenges in scalability, long-term consistency, and handling complex, multi-hop knowledge updates.
The field lacks standardized benchmarks and evaluation protocols, making fair comparisons between methods difficult.
Knowledge editing has practical applications in correcting misinformation, personalizing models, and maintaining up-to-date AI systems.
future_direction: Improving the scalability and efficiency of KME methods for mass editing.
Developing KME techniques for multimodal large language models.
Ensuring the long-term consistency and reliability of edited knowledge over sequential edits.
Addressing the challenge of editing complex, multi-hop knowledge and reasoning chains.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have recently transformed both the academic and industrial landscapes due to their remarkable capacity to understand, analyze, and generate texts based on their vast knowledge and reasoning ability. Nevertheless, one major drawback of LLMs is their substantial computational cost for pre-training due to their unprecedented amounts of parameters. The disadvantage is exacerbated when new knowledge frequently needs to be introduced into the pre-trained model. Therefore, it is imperative to develop effective and efficient techniques to update pre-trained LLMs. Traditional methods encode new knowledge in pre-trained LLMs through direct fine-tuning. However, naively re-training LLMs can be computationally intensive and risks degenerating valuable pre-trained knowledge irrelevant to the update in the model. Recently, Knowledge-based Model Editing (KME) has attracted increasing attention, which aims to precisely modify the LLMs to incorporate specific knowledge, without negatively influencing other irrelevant knowledge. In this survey, we aim to provide a comprehensive and in-depth overview of recent advances in the field of KME. We first introduce a general formulation of KME to encompass different KME strategies. Afterward, we provide an innovative taxonomy of KME techniques based on how the new knowledge is introduced into pre-trained LLMs, and investigate existing KME strategies while analyzing key insights, advantages, and limitations of methods from each category. Moreover, representative metrics, datasets, and applications of KME are introduced accordingly. Finally, we provide an in-depth analysis regarding the practicality and remaining challenges of KME and suggest promising research directions for further advancement in this field.

papers.title: Knowledge Graph Enhanced Large Language Model Editing
papers.research_question: How can we improve model editing by capturing associated knowledge changes using knowledge graphs to enhance the generalization ability of post-edit LLMs?
papers.core_contribution: The paper proposes GLAME, a novel model editing method that leverages knowledge graphs to capture associated knowledge changes, thereby improving the generalization capability of post-edit LLMs.
papers.conclusion: GLAME is an effective model editing method that leverages knowledge graphs to capture associated knowledge changes, enhancing the generalization ability of post-edit LLMs.
papers.key_findings:
GLAME outperforms state-of-the-art editing methods, especially in Portability Score, indicating better generalization for multi-hop reasoning.
Ablation studies show that the Graph-based Knowledge Edit (GKE) module and relational information in the graph are crucial for performance.
The method is sensitive to hyperparameters like subgraph order and number of neighbors, with optimal performance at moderate values.
Directly editing high-order relationships without the GKE module degrades performance, highlighting the importance of structured integration.
GLAME effectively captures associated knowledge changes, leading to improved performance on multi-hop questions in MQUAKE.
papers.limitation: The framework's reliance on knowledge graphs may be limited by the availability and quality of relevant knowledge; poor quality or scarce knowledge can degrade performance.
future_direction: Develop more sophisticated subgraph sampling strategies to improve subgraph quality and more accurately capture knowledge changes resulting from editing.
Increase sampling speed and reduce subgraph size.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are pivotal in advancing natural language processing (NLP) tasks, yet their efficacy is hampered by inaccuracies and outdated knowledge. Model editing emerges as a promising solution to address these challenges. However, existing editing methods struggle to track and incorporate changes in knowledge associated with edits, which limits the generalization ability of postedit LLMs in processing edited knowledge. To tackle these problems, we propose a novel model editing method that leverages knowledge graphs for enhancing LLM editing, namely GLAME. Specifically, we first utilize a knowledge graph augmentation module to uncover associated knowledge that has changed due to editing, obtaining its internal representations within LLMs. This approach allows knowledge alterations within LLMs to be reflected through an external graph structure. Subsequently, we design a graph-based knowledge edit module to integrate structured knowledge into the model editing.
